operator_plays.name: Forced-Pooling Docket & Non-Consent Mineral Lease Curve-Jumping Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Use public pooling applications and drilling schedules to identify unleased mineral interests before election deadlines, pricing royalty upside against title defects and non-consent cost exposure.
inputs: State pooling dockets and election orders
Mineral ownership chain and lease abstracts
Operator development plans and local lease comparables
workflow: 1. Monitor pooling applications and map affected mineral tracts and hearing dates
2. Verify net mineral acres, ownership authority, and election consequences with specialist counsel
3. Negotiate disclosed lease or option terms and fund obligations before applicable deadlines
4. Assign permitted interests or administer royalty receipts with division-order reconciliation
metrics: Net royalty or assignment proceeds per invested dollar

platform_risks.failure_mode: Missed election or unexpected non-consent penalty
platform_risks.trigger: Stale docket feed or misread state-specific pooling order
platform_risks.impact: Delayed royalties and unbudgeted development-cost exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unverified order changes and days remaining to election
platform_risks.fallback: Stop acquisitions pending counsel review and choose only timely, fully understood permitted elections

operator_plays.name: Fractional Heir-Share Acquisition & Tenancy-in-Common Partition Buyout Forcing
operator_plays.mechanism: Acquire documented fractional heir interests at a discount reflecting illiquidity, then seek consensual buyouts or counsel-supervised partition subject to heirs-property protections and co-owner rights.
inputs: Probate files and verified heirship records
Title chain, occupancy facts, and independent appraisal
Applicable partition and heirs-property protection rules
workflow: 1. Establish ownership fractions, probate authority, and encumbrances before contacting sellers
2. Provide transparent offers with independent-advice opportunity and modeled partition costs
3. Seek voluntary co-owner buyouts or an agreed market sale before considering litigation
4. If unresolved, use counsel-led statutory procedures honoring notice, appraisal, and buyout rights
metrics: Net proceeds after carrying and legal costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: Heirs-property protections defeat assumed forced-sale economics
platform_risks.trigger: Mandatory co-owner buyout, partition-in-kind preference, or defective heirship
platform_risks.impact: Long holding period and lower realizable value
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unresolved heirs and statutory buyout conditions per property
platform_risks.fallback: Renegotiate voluntary exits or retain the interest without threatening unavailable remedies

operator_plays.name: Cell-Tower, Rooftop & Billboard Perpetual Easement Strip-Out Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Separate assignable site-access and rent rights from underlying real estate for specialist buyers, pricing tenant termination rights and the permanent burden left on the residual property.
inputs: Tower, rooftop, and billboard leases and amendments
Title, lender consent, and zoning documents
Specialist easement-buyer bids and residual property appraisals
workflow: 1. Identify leased sites and reconcile actual rent receipts with termination and renewal terms
2. Verify assignment rights, mortgage restrictions, maintenance duties, and required consents
3. Compare easement sale proceeds against lost rent and residual property impairment
4. Close approved conveyances through escrow and record access, utilities, and rent-allocation rights
metrics: Net easement proceeds versus retained rent value

platform_risks.failure_mode: Nonassignable lease or excessive permanent property burden
platform_risks.trigger: Missing tenant or lender consent or easement scope exceeding valued rights
platform_risks.impact: Failed closing or reduced refinancing and resale value
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unresolved consent conditions and residual appraisal discount
platform_risks.fallback: Retain the lease or negotiate a narrower term-limited assignment with all required approvals

operator_plays.name: FERC / ISO Substation Interconnection Queue & Powered-Land Option Flipping
operator_plays.mechanism: Overlay public interconnection queues with land-use and substation data to option potentially useful sites, treating queue position and nearby infrastructure as signals rather than guaranteed deliverable power.
inputs: ISO and utility interconnection queues and study results
Parcel zoning, transmission corridors, and substation maps
Utility service estimates and developer site requirements
workflow: 1. Match queue activity and infrastructure constraints to suitable parcels
2. Verify site control requirements, zoning, environmental limits, and utility capacity assumptions
3. Negotiate assignable diligence-contingent options within capped carrying-cost budgets
4. Assign approved options to qualified developers with explicit disclosure of unresolved power and study conditions
metrics: Option cost per qualified developable acre
Net assignment proceeds after study and option costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: Queue withdrawal or prohibitive network upgrade cost
platform_risks.trigger: Restudy, milestone failure, or capacity estimate unsupported by utility commitments
platform_risks.impact: Option expiry and unrecoverable diligence spending
platform_risks.detection_metric: Study cost revisions and unresolved interconnection milestones
platform_risks.fallback: Let contingent options lapse or reposition land for independently viable uses without claiming secured power

operator_plays.name: TCPA Serial-Plaintiff Docket Scraping & Real-Time Litigator-Scrub Firewall Tollbooth
operator_plays.mechanism: Offer consent-first outbound compliance screening using lawful docket-derived risk signals alongside mandatory do-not-call and revocation checks; plaintiff matching neither authorizes contact nor replaces TCPA compliance.
inputs: Permitted public docket data with identity confidence scores
Consent provenance, revocations, and suppression lists
Applicable calling rules and customer retention policies
workflow: 1. Ingest permitted docket records with source dates, minimization, and human identity review
2. Check consent, do-not-call status, revocations, and calling restrictions before optional risk enrichment
3. Suppress noncompliant contacts and route uncertain matches to review without planting honeypots or provoking claims
4. Serve auditable screening decisions with correction, deletion, and retention controls
metrics: Contacts blocked for missing consent or suppression match

platform_risks.failure_mode: False identity match or false assurance of permission to call
platform_risks.trigger: Stale docket data or treating absence from a plaintiff list as consent
platform_risks.impact: Unlawful outreach, privacy complaints, and customer liability
platform_risks.detection_metric: Consent-audit failure rate and upheld identity correction requests
platform_risks.fallback: Disable uncertain enrichment and require independently verified consent and authoritative suppression checks

positioning_alternatives.title: The Decimal Audit

positioning_alternatives.title: Royalty Over Bonus
positioning_alternatives.subtitle: Negotiate the lease once, because your heirs live with it for decades
positioning_alternatives.audience: Unleased mineral owners facing landman offers, pooling notices and term royalty deeds
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: Sands prices a fair bonus at mineral value divided by 2 or 3 and favors the highest royalty rate. He shows a $6,000/NMA offer is only $3,000/NRA, and that a 25% royalty doubles sale value over 12.5%.
positioning_alternatives.validation_status: Grounded strictly in Vol. 023 YouTube practitioner transcripts.

positioning_alternatives.title: Follow the Drill Bit

positioning_alternatives.audience: Mineral buyers, sellers weighing a lump sum, and investors building monthly royalty income
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: Sands discounts producing minerals at about 10% and pays 36-60x monthly royalty for old flat wells. Hatcher's $95,000 PDP buy recouped 40% in nine months. Both insist on title work and PSA review before any money moves.

chapters.question_prompt: What exactly do I own: minerals, royalties, NPRIs or overrides, and how are those interests created, measured and conveyed?
chapters.title: What You Actually Own: Mineral Estates, Royalties and Their Carve-Outs
chapters.subtitle: Severance from the surface, mineral vs. royalty ownership, net mineral acres vs. net royalty acres, gross vs. net acreage, fixed vs. floating NPRIs, overriding royalty interests, and conveying royalties vs. mineral interests
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Matt Sands to Steven Hatcher, LMJ Land Services, PetroPeak Investments, and the Energy Law Professor agree on the core map: minerals are real property severed by deed, the mineral owner holds the executive right to lease and collect bonus, and every carve-out below that strips rights. Royalty and NPRI holders get production but no lease, bonus, or rentals; the ORRI is carved from the working interest and dies with the lease. Street math runs on three numbers: net mineral acres, royalty decimal, and net royalty acres, with Sands showing a $6,000 per NMA offer is only $3,000 per NRA at 25%. The fights are over wording: fixed versus floating NPRIs, where Van Dyke put about $44 million on one reading, and whether a small royalty beats a mineral interest with future-development upside.

key_metrics.context: Hatcher's stated range for the royalty a mineral owner receives, paid monthly for 10 to 50-plus years while the well produces.

key_metrics.metric: Royalty Cash Flow Decline on a 35.5 NMA Deal

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner starts from the same foundation: minerals are real property, and what you actually own depends on which sticks of the bundle your deed carried. Matt Sands explains that US minerals were originally granted to surface owners in fee simple, pass by will or deed, and need a legal description that is 'sufficient' [3AnqzZSRGtg @ 00:01:54]. Steven Hatcher defines severance as the moment the mineral estate is created separate and apart from the surface, triggered when it is granted or reserved in a conveyance instrument, which he calls basically a deed. A mineral deed hands over the entire estate, royalties plus the executive rights to grant leases and receive bonuses, while the royalty deed is the second type he names [b13q6ndzbZM @ 00:01:02]. Hatcher adds that mineral rights are themselves a subdividable stick. Sands sorts owners into four positions: fee simple owners who can lease, severed mineral owners who keep necessary surface use, surface owners who cannot lease, and royalty owners who get no lease, no bonus, and no rentals [3AnqzZSRGtg @ 00:04:23]. The Venergy Momentum speaker draws the street conclusion from the dominant mineral estate: do not buy surface alone, and when you sell surface, reserve the minerals in the sale [175xk8ZQHpI @ 00:01:45].

On the cash side, the speakers agree a royalty is a cost-free cut of gross revenue whose percentage gets set in the lease. Steven Hatcher puts the range at 12.5% to 25% of gross well revenue, with checks arriving monthly for as long as the well produces, anywhere from 10 to 50-plus years [WZxmCcTgeWk @ 00:00:49]. LandApp by LandGate says royalties bear no operating costs and are usually stated as an eighth or a sixth, while the lease bonus is a one-time payment [r7MMN5ueVCs @ 00:00:55]. John Jordan of PetroPeak Investments lines up mineral, royalty, and ORRI owners as three positions that all get paid without funding drilling, though he flags that taxes and post-production deductions may still apply [zHSS1bvXiNk @ 00:02:58]. The consensus on the shape of that money is blunt: it declines. Hatcher compares royalties to rents or annuities, only more volatile because they ride oil and gas prices, and calls it a declining stream unlike investments that stay flat or appreciate. The Venergy Momentum speaker agrees wells can produce 20 to 50 years, but most revenue lands in years one through five and re-stimulation bumps are short-lived [175xk8ZQHpI @ 00:03:56]. Venergy adds that most companies don't pay until your account hits $100 or more.

The carve-outs are where the consensus gets sharpest. Matt Sands, John Jordan, and Blue Mesa Minerals all place the overriding royalty inside the working interest rather than the minerals, and all three say it dies with the lease; Sands names geologists, landmen, engineers, and brokers as the usual holders [pjmqehPUgL8 @ 00:01:31]. Blue Mesa calls an ORRI an interest in the proceeds of the sale of oil and gas, free from the cost of production, and once the wells go uneconomic and the lease is released, both the royalty and the ORRI are gone [PR8LyKmo8S4 @ 00:00:37]. The non-participating royalty interest sits on the other side of the line: Sands says it is carved from the mineral estate and perpetual, while the ORRI expires with the lease [qru8bh4mMms @ 00:10:28]. Sands notes owners create NPRIs to raise cash or as gifts to grandkids. Jordan, Sands, and the Energy Law Professor agree the NPRI holder takes a share of production with no leasing rights, no bonus, and no delay rental. LMJ Land Services makes it concrete with Carl, who holds an NPRI under Bob's half: Carl can't sign the lease, gets no bonus, and no delay rentals, and his net mineral acres are zero [IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:00:40].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The first number to nail is net mineral acres, and every speaker computes it the same way: gross acres times your fractional interest. Tracy Lenz warns that the 320 gross acres in a description like Dawson County, Section 39, Block 35, Township 4 is just the fence, not what you own, and that the '$10' consideration on a deed is not the actual sale price [9zqL93Kdy1I @ 00:01:06]. To find your real share, Lenz either traces title back to patent or backs into it from the payment: 50% of 320 gross acres is 160 NMA [9zqL93Kdy1I @ 00:03:39]. Matt Sands defines one NMA as 100% of the minerals under one acre and runs a 160-acre quarter at a 1/10 interest to 16 NMA [iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:03:23]. LMJ Land Services applies the same formula to a 160-acre tract split between Ann and Bob, giving each 80 NMA and Carl, the NPRI holder, zero, which is why the bonus goes to Ann and Bob only [IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:00:40]. Lenz compares undivided interest to owning shares of Google: you own a slice of the whole tract, not a fenced corner, so 10% of a 100-acre ranch is 10 NMA.

Next comes the royalty decimal, which LMJ Land Services computes as mineral interest times lease royalty, so Ann's half under a 1/4 lease is .125. Carl's NPRI is where the money moves. Read as a fixed 1/16, Carl gets .03125 carved out of Bob's share, leaving Bob .09375; read as a floating 'one half of the royalty,' Carl and Bob each get .0625, with Hysaw and Van Dyke cited [IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:01:41]. 'Same tract, two readings, and Carl's decimal doubles.' LMJ's control check: Ann plus Bob plus Carl has to equal the lease royalty of .25, and if it doesn't, go back to the deeds [IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:02:02]. Matt Sands runs the same split on a 1/5 NPRI under a 25% lease: fixed gives the NPRI owner 20% and the mineral owner 5%, while floating flips it to 5% and 20% [qru8bh4mMms @ 00:14:25]. His drafting tell is that 'of all the oil and gas' reads fixed and 'of the royalty' reads floating, with 'usual 1/8' language as the twist. Oliva Gibbs shows the stakes: a fixed 1/16 stays 1/16 whether the lease is 1/8 or 25%, and Van Dyke put about $44 million on the reading [QPk4GTvt5YU @ 00:12:22].

Net royalty acres is the normalizing tool buyers and owners use to compare offers apples to apples. Matt Sands defines one NRA as 1/8 of 8/8, or 12.5%, under one acre, and gives the formula: NRA equals NMA times royalty rate times eight [iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:05:59]. His worked offer: 16 NMA at a 25% royalty is 32 NRA, so a $6,000-per-NMA offer, $96,000 total, is really only $3,000 per NRA, while the neighbor's $5,000 per NMA at 1/8 is $5,000 per NRA [iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:09:06]. Burdened tracts take one more step: subtract the NPRI from your royalty, then divide by 12.5%. Tracy Lenz runs a sibling case: same NMA, but the sister leased at 25% and the brother at 20%, so her acres are worth more, and normalized to the old 1/8 standard she holds 20 NRA [37dcxhS1a6E @ 00:04:32]. Sands also flags 'assuming 25%' offers: $10,000 per acre at 25% is about $5,000 at 12.5%. On rate versus bonus, Sands compares $500 per NMA at 3/16 to $250 at 20 to 25% and says almost always take zero bonus and the highest royalty [qru8bh4mMms @ 00:09:06].

callout.title: How Operators Squeeze the Numbers
callout.body: Four moves the practitioners use to avoid getting priced on the wrong number or sold at the wrong time.
items: On unleased minerals, ask the buyer which royalty rate the offer assumes; if the going rate is 15-20% against their 12.5%, there is negotiation room [Matt Sands — iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:14:51]
Run the sum check on every tract: Ann plus Bob plus Carl has to equal the lease royalty, and if it doesn't, go back to the deeds [LMJ Land Services — IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:02:02]

Many ORRIs are sold in the first two or three months of production, at peak volumes and before anyone knows how the well will settle, which usually generates more cash [Blue Mesa Minerals — PR8LyKmo8S4 @ 00:00:37]
When taking an ORRI assignment, add protective language against washout, and value an old single well on existing production only [Matt Sands — pjmqehPUgL8 @ 00:07:10]

sop_steps.title: Trace the Deed Chain to Severance
sop_steps.action: Pull every conveyance back to patent and mark where the minerals were severed or reserved.
sop_steps.detail: Hatcher pins severance to the grant or reservation of the mineral estate in a conveyance instrument, and Lenz traces title back to patent while ignoring the '$10' consideration line [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — b13q6ndzbZM @ 00:00:17] [Tracy Lenz — 9zqL93Kdy1I @ 00:02:42]

sop_steps.title: Compute NMA and the Royalty Decimal
sop_steps.action: Multiply gross acres by your fractional interest, then multiply your interest by the lease royalty.
sop_steps.detail: LMJ's 160-acre tract gives Ann and Bob 80 NMA each, Ann's decimal comes out at .125, and every owner's decimal must sum to the .25 lease royalty [LMJ Land Services — IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:02:02]

sop_steps.title: Classify Every Carve-Out by Its Wording
sop_steps.action: Read each reservation for fixed versus floating language and mineral versus royalty language.
sop_steps.detail: Sands reads 'of all the oil and gas' as fixed and 'of the royalty' as floating, and the Energy Law Professor treats 'in and under' as a mineral interest and 'produced and saved' as a royalty [Matt Sands — qru8bh4mMms @ 00:17:44] [Energy Law Professor — OYaKeqiMHWc @ 00:29:01]

sop_steps.title: Verify Payout and Normalize Every Offer
sop_steps.action: Check wells on the state commission site, chase suspense funds, and convert offers to dollars per NRA.
sop_steps.detail: Sands checks state commission wells and calls the operator's owner relations about suspense funds, then runs NRA equals NMA times royalty rate times eight before comparing bids [Matt Sands — pjmqehPUgL8 @ 00:23:49] [Matt Sands — iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:06:20]

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether a small mineral interest or a straight royalty is the better asset to hold. Energy Law Professor walks through McSwain v. Musselshell, a 1981 Montana fight where 1933 and 1943 instruments reserved 2.5% of the minerals but a 1944 deed reserved a 2.5% royalty. The appellate court reversed the district court because a 2.5% mineral interest under a 1/8 lease yields far less than a 2.5% royalty, and concluded the royalty 'usually is' better in reality [OYaKeqiMHWc @ 00:11:16]. John Jordan of PetroPeak Investments argues the other side of the ledger. Minerals carry future leasing and development rights, so they can hold value even with little current production, such as additional horizontal wells targeting other formations [zHSS1bvXiNk @ 00:02:07]. Jordan then hedges his own pitch. He warns that future drilling is not guaranteed because plans change, prices fluctuate, and owners may wait years, so minerals in an active horizontal play do not automatically beat declining wells under an ORRI [zHSS1bvXiNk @ 00:09:28]. Matt Sands settles the leasing version of the fight with a cash-flow rule. Offered $500/NMA at 3/16 versus $250 at 20 to 25%, he says it is almost always better to take zero bonus and the highest royalty rate, because the rate directly drives the value of the minerals going forward [qru8bh4mMms @ 00:09:06].

Whether an NPRI is fixed or floating is where the money swings hardest, and the outcome depends on the state and the exact words in the deed. LMJ Land Services runs one 160-acre tract with a 1/4 lease royalty. Read as fixed, Carl's 1/16 NPRI yields .03125, which comes out of Bob's share. Read as floating ('one half of the royalty'), Carl and Bob each take .0625, so 'Carl's decimal doubles' on the same tract [IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:01:41]. Matt Sands gives the working rule of thumb: 'of all the oil and gas' means fixed and 'of the royalty' means floating. He adds that the 'usual 1/8' language is a twist and that interpretation varies by state [qru8bh4mMms @ 00:17:44]. Oliva Gibbs shows how far Texas courts will push toward floating. In Van Dyke, with roughly $44M at stake, the lower courts said 1/16, the Texas Supreme Court said 1/2, and the presumption can be rebutted only from the document itself [QPk4GTvt5YU @ 00:13:17]. Ohio runs the other way in Gibbs's account. In Crum, the word 'his' made the interest a fixed 1/16. Mineral Development v. SWN held the 1/32 and 1/16 fixed and not reduced by the lease royalty. The Seventh District rejects any 1/8 presumption, and the Ohio Supreme Court has not ruled [QPk4GTvt5YU @ 00:39:11].

On overrides and offers, the playbooks split between sellers and buyers. Blue Mesa Minerals reports that a lot of ORRIs are sold in the first two or three months of production, at peak output and before anyone knows how the well will settle, and that selling early usually generates more cash for the holder [PR8LyKmo8S4 @ 00:00:54]. Matt Sands applies a buyer's discipline to an old single well: value it on existing production only, and add protective language to the assignment against washout risk [pjmqehPUgL8 @ 00:05:20]. John Jordan frames the same tension as identical checks hiding different rights. $100,000 gross at a 20% royalty creates a $20,000 burden, and a 10% holder of that burden gets $2,000 a month. A 2% ORRI on the same gross also gets $2,000, yet the override usually dies with the lease while the minerals persist [zHSS1bvXiNk @ 00:07:53]. On pricing, Sands buys in dollars per NMA with reduction terms for burdens, but he coaches sellers to convert everything to net royalty acres. At 16 NMA under a 25% royalty, the tract becomes 32 NRA. A $6,000/NMA offer, $96,000 total, then shrinks to $3,000 per NRA, even though that royalty pays twice the neighbor's [iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:09:06].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common trap is trusting a number nobody has reconciled. LMJ Land Services runs a hard check on every tract: Ann, plus Bob, plus Carl must equal the lease royalty of .25. If the decimals do not sum, the analyst goes back to the deeds rather than forcing the math, and the report shows the volume, page, and quoted NPRI language [IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:02:02]. Tracy Lenz warns that the deed itself misleads. The '$10' consideration is not the actual sale price, and 320 gross acres in a Dawson County section is the fence, not ownership. She finds net mineral acres by tracing back to patent or by backing into the figure from payment, so 50% of 320 equals 160 NMA [9zqL93Kdy1I @ 00:03:39]. Matt Sands reports that 'attorneys aren't perfect' and tells owners to keep their own documents, because an operator change can trigger a fresh title review. He also notes that Texas alone requires a signed division order, with suspense acceptable while title is resolved [qru8bh4mMms @ 00:22:33]. Steven Hatcher adds that the conveyance instrument controls everything downstream. Severance happens at the moment a deed grants or reserves the mineral estate, and a mineral deed carrying executive rights differs from a royalty deed [b13q6ndzbZM @ 00:00:17].

The second trap is pricing a royalty like a flat annuity. Steven Hatcher calls royalties more volatile than rents because they ride oil and gas prices. His own deal on 35.5 NMA at a 25% royalty, with six new wells planned, projected roughly $600,000 in Year 1, about $250,000 in Year 2, and about $20,000 by Year 10, which he contrasts with real estate's 10-to-30-year payback [WZxmCcTgeWk @ 00:02:58]. Venergy Momentum Oil & Gas confirms the curve from the owner side. Wells can produce 20 to 50 years, but most revenue lands in years one through five, re-stimulation bumps are short-lived, and most companies do not pay until the account hits $100 or greater [175xk8ZQHpI @ 00:03:56]. Blue Mesa Minerals spells out the terminal event for overrides: once the wells are uneconomic, the lease is released, which kills both the royalty and the ORRI under it [PR8LyKmo8S4 @ 00:00:37]. John Jordan's due-diligence answer at PetroPeak is a full review of existing wells, declines, remaining reserves, operators, ownership rights, lease terms, and development potential. He then matches the purchase price to the remaining economic life rather than to the current monthly check [zHSS1bvXiNk @ 00:10:57].

The third trap is the counterparty, or the paperwork, quietly reshaping the deal. Matt Sands warns that buyers may exploit owners' unfamiliarity with these metrics. An offer of '$10,000/acre assuming 25%' is only about $5,000 at 12.5%, so with unleased minerals he tells owners to ask which royalty rate the buyer assumed. A going rate of 15 to 20% against the buyer's 12.5% is negotiation room [iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:11:18]. On NPRIs, Sands flags dependency risk: the NPRI owner rides on whatever lease terms the executive negotiates and cannot sign the lease [qru8bh4mMms @ 00:04:54]. For overrides, his checklist starts with proportionate reduction: 1/2 times 1/8 equals 1/16, while a '1/8 of 8/8' override is not reduced. It continues with literal interpretation, depth limits, deductions, pooling consent, state commission well records, and calls to the operator's owner relations about suspense funds [pjmqehPUgL8 @ 00:24:59]. Even polished pitches contain slips. John Jordan states that royalty owners bear no drilling or operating cost, then says they 'generally are responsible for paying their share of the drilling and completion costs.' That line contradicts his own earlier point and Blue Mesa's cost-free description of overrides [zHSS1bvXiNk @ 00:03:30].

callout.title: Do not price, sign, or sell until these four checks clear
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, reversal, or bottleneck the practitioners hit in live deals and title work.
items: Reconcile every owner's decimal back to the lease royalty, and pull the deeds whenever the sum misses [LMJ Land Services — IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:02:02].

action_checklist: Compute NMA as gross acres times your fractional interest, then convert to NRA as NMA times royalty times eight [Matt Sands — iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:06:20].
Subtract any NPRI from your royalty rate before dividing by 12.5% to get true net royalty acres [Matt Sands — iVFjOPF8JW0 @ 00:13:39].
Quote the exact NPRI wording and test whether it reads 'of all the oil and gas' (fixed) or 'of the royalty' (floating) [Matt Sands — qru8bh4mMms @ 00:17:44].
Confirm the decimals of all owners on the tract sum to the lease royalty before accepting a division order [LMJ Land Services — IBxLIQjDNto @ 00:02:02].
When leasing, weigh zero bonus with the highest royalty rate against a larger one-time bonus at a lower rate [Matt Sands — qru8bh4mMms @ 00:09:06].
When selling surface, reserve the minerals in the sale, because the mineral estate is dominant [Venergy Momentum Oil & Gas — 175xk8ZQHpI @ 00:02:48].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I find my minerals on a map, research nearby wells and organize my ownership records using free and paid tools?
chapters.title: Locating, Researching and Inventorying Your Minerals
chapters.subtitle: Mapping tracts and legal descriptions, Texas RRC, Oklahoma Corporation Commission and North Dakota data sites, WellDatabase, Enverus spacing tools, mineral title searches, AI-built deed inventories, and organizing a mineral legacy
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the first job is knowing exactly what you own: pull the legal description from the source deed, plot it on a free state GIS, and log every tract in one spreadsheet with interest type, net acres, lease status, and provenance. Mineral title runs on a separate chain from the surface, and a royalty check never cures a recorded gap. Street mechanics are state-specific: the Texas RRC viewer with 8-digit API entry, Oklahoma's OCC map plus OkTAP PUN severance records, and North Dakota's $50-a-year Basic paywall, which Matt Sands sidesteps with WellDatabase's free tier. Paid help runs about $600 a day for a landman and $3,000 for a limited title search. Sands and Justin Williams push AI for run sheets but demand spot-checks, while Dave of titlesearch.com insists only a dedicated mineral search exposes split-off rights.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner here starts in the same place: before leasing, selling, or auditing a check, pin down exactly what you own. Blue Mesa Minerals calls knowing what you own 'the most important thing to managing your minerals' and says the best opening move is to pull the legal description and look at it on a map [PAfHHmByY2I @ 00:06:23]. Steven Hatcher, an oil and gas attorney with more than a decade in the business, labels it part one of minerals management and warns that owners who skip it are 'Flying Blind' and open themselves up to 'being on the bad end of a deal' [5hXDw_OFeQc @ 00:01:01]. Matt Sands and Justin Williams run the whole workflow in strict order: know what you own, learn the interest types, map the activity, and only then put a value on it [u4xA0UNrxQs @ 00:03:12]. NARO frames the same discipline as a pre-signature check: verify which rights a document actually touches and who the person contacting you represents, because leasing and selling are different transactions [o8FqhVu6MNM @ 00:00:33]. The trigger in the field is almost always external, a landman's leasing offer or a cold call to an heir who never knew the interest existed, which is exactly why the inventory has to be built before that phone rings rather than after it.

The second point of agreement is that mineral ownership lives on its own paper trail. Dave of titlesearch.com, speaking on AFX, says mineral rights are subsurface, 'do not run with the land,' and 'run on a separate chain of title,' so a standard search shows only the surface chain and a special mineral rights search is needed to surface them [JpHijIsWFL4 @ 00:01:50]. Rights can split off in any transfer, and probate and heirship gaps are common. NARO hits the same gap from the payment side: 'A royalty statement is a starting point, not a complete ownership record,' and 'A check in your name doesn't resolve a gap in the recorded chain of ownership' [o8FqhVu6MNM @ 00:04:48]. The prescribed move is to search county records by grantor and grantee and to ask the paying company which records and calculations support its decimal. Hatcher sends owners straight back to the source deed to extract the legal description rather than trusting secondhand summaries or a buyer's letter [5hXDw_OFeQc @ 00:03:43]. Sands and Williams add that deeds and leases are the documents that matter most when an heir reconstructs an inheritance, and that a missing deed into a trust or an unrecorded probate step leaves the family exposed to the same chain-of-title hole the title searchers keep finding [yfXV7bIliEk @ 00:09:25].

Practitioners also converge on one consolidated inventory. Sands and Williams want a single spreadsheet logging state, county, legal description, interest type, decimal or net acres, lease status, and provenance, and they point to a NARO member who needed 18 months to untangle an inheritance from boxes stacked to the ceiling, alongside their figure that executors average 16 months settling estates [yfXV7bIliEk @ 00:09:57]. Their timing play is the holidays, when families are together, the pace is slower, and people are reflective enough to walk through that sheet. Blue Mesa keeps a parallel physical file: one folder with leases, division orders, and a single sample statement, plus a free mineral spreadsheet the firm hands out [PAfHHmByY2I @ 00:06:41]. Sands admits that, looking back, they 'would absolutely keep everything that might be related to it' [u4xA0UNrxQs @ 00:11:17]. The math that fills the net-acre column is agreed and simple: NARO's worked example takes the NE/4 at 160 gross acres times a 1/8 mineral share to land at 20 net mineral acres held undivided across the whole tract, and it stresses that a 1/8 mineral share is not the same thing as a 1/8 royalty, so the spreadsheet needs separate columns for mineral fraction and lease royalty rate [o8FqhVu6MNM @ 00:03:04].

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: In Texas the workhorse is the Railroad Commission GIS viewer. Sands says to Google 'Texas rrc GIS' or open it from rc.texas.gov, ignore the district regions, then either zoom down to block and section or hit the magnifying-glass search and choose Surveys [gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:03:38]. Inputs are county plus survey name, block and section, or the abstract number; most deeds omit the abstract, so once you find it, write it down (A112 in the demo) for faster repeat searches. The legend reads: a line through the symbol is a plugged oil well, a solid green dot is producing, a red starburst is gas, and a hollow blue circle is a permit. For API lookups, drop the leading '42' and enter the 3-digit county code plus the 5-digit well ID, 8 digits total [gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:08:29]. Blue Mesa runs the same viewer on Glascock County abstract 792 with no block or section needed, flags an 'H' suffix as a horizontal well, and warns production data runs a couple of months behind [PAfHHmByY2I @ 00:02:09]. Tracy Lenz, a petroleum engineer and certified mineral appraiser, stresses Texas is not a PLSS state, so tracts read survey, block, section; quarter calls like SW/4 of SE/4 are read backwards, and appraisal-district maps confirm which way is north [yEKUUQ-zkaU @ 00:10:43].

Oklahoma and North Dakota take more clicks. Williams calls Oklahoma 'trickier'; the path is OCC, Divisions, Oil & Gas Conservation, then the OCC Well Data Finder map, searched by section in STR format such as '01 11N 02W' [GS_N0TTrBPY @ 00:05:27]. On the demo tract the NW/4 of Sec 1-11N-2W has no surface location, yet the Roller 1-36H bottom hole sits in Sec 1, and the 480-acre horizontal unit yields a decimal of net mineral acres divided by 480 times the lease royalty rate. Official production lives in the Oklahoma Tax Commission OkTAP PUN search, the severance-tax record: drop state code '35,' use county 109, oil product code 1 and gas code 5; the demo pulls 1,343.43 bbl for September 2023 [GS_N0TTrBPY @ 00:13:44]. North Dakota paywalls its data through dmr.nd.gov: the GIS viewer is free, Basic adds permits, plats, well files, and production for $50 a year, and Advanced adds pooling and spacing orders, downloads, and hearing audio [1HDBzjGoDdc @ 00:16:47]. Sands' free workaround is a WellDatabase account, which shows production view-only a couple of days behind, and co-founder John Farrell says the free Lite plan carries well headers, production, permits, completions, frac, construction, and formations [EDD6HaFdEzE @ 00:20:59].

Paid research gets rationed hard. Sands and Williams say county services charge per download or per page, so search for free and buy only chain-of-title instruments: mineral, quitclaim and warranty deeds, leases, assignments, ratifications, and memoranda, skipping mortgages and refinances as noise [u4xA0UNrxQs @ 00:12:41]. When the work goes to a professional, a landman starts around $600 a day and a limited title search runs about a week and roughly $3,000. Sands' WellDatabase play is to pay one month of Essential at $250 for decline curve analysis, then downgrade, replacing a $600 to $800 consultant; Farrell adds that Essential exports up to 10,000 wells and that an owner facing a buyer should upgrade for just that month [EDD6HaFdEzE @ 00:03:52]. For digitizing old paper, Sands converted a 50-year-old Exhibit A into Excel with AI, computing fractions like 1/12 times 1/160, but insists on spot-checking because early ChatGPT invented case law that 'didn't exist' [NkT15qxxGYM @ 00:14:34]. Hatcher's map recipe on the free Louisiana GIS stacks townships, sections, roads, Haynesville units, wells without busy serial labels, then bottom holes and bores, which on the 120-acre FJ tract exposed 6 wells in Sec 1 and 4 in Sec 2 [5hXDw_OFeQc @ 00:08:12].

callout.title: Reading the public data like an auditor
callout.body: The state sites hand you raw numbers that do not match a royalty statement line for line. These are the adjustments and checks the practitioners run before trusting any figure.
items: RRC gas volumes are wet gas while royalty statements show dry gas plus NGLs after shrinkage, so treat the commission figure as an approximation and expect paid volume to be lower [Matt Sands — gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:27:03].

Texas reports production at the lease level, so add up the wells yourself and read the disposition column for sold volume; April 2012 showed 1,990 bbl produced but 1,905 sold [Matt Sands — gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:25:22].
A Mineral IQ alert for a new permit or rig within a 2-mile radius does not prove you hold an interest; verify it against the permit and the plat before acting [Matt Sands — GS_N0TTrBPY @ 00:02:49].
When feeding division orders to ChatGPT or Claude, redact your Social Security number first and pay for a tier that lets you opt out of training on your data [Matt Sands — NkT15qxxGYM @ 00:34:48].

sop_steps.title: Extract the legal description
sop_steps.action: Pull the section, township and range, survey and block, or metes and bounds call from the source deed.
sop_steps.detail: Hatcher identifies three description types, PLSS, subdivision, and metes and bounds, and says to find the description in your source deed before touching a map [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — 5hXDw_OFeQc @ 00:03:43].

sop_steps.title: Plot the tract on the state GIS
sop_steps.action: Search the state viewer by survey, block, section, or abstract and record the abstract number once found.
sop_steps.detail: On the Texas RRC viewer, enter county plus survey name, block and section, or abstract number, then note the abstract (A112 in the demo) because most deeds omit it [Matt Sands — gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:05:18].

sop_steps.title: Read the unit and compute your decimal
sop_steps.action: Open the spacing order and plat, confirm unit size, and divide net mineral acres by gross unit acres.
sop_steps.detail: For the Oklahoma demo, the 480-acre horizontal unit gives a decimal of net mineral acres divided by 480 times the lease royalty rate [Matt Sands — GS_N0TTrBPY @ 00:08:36].

sop_steps.title: Audit production against checks
sop_steps.action: Compare official production to statements and treat a production drop as the trigger to pull the well file.
sop_steps.detail: In North Dakota a rod pump installed in November 2018 with only 15 producing days shows why a production drop is your trigger to open the well file [Matt Sands — 1HDBzjGoDdc @ 00:12:42].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fork is who does the digging. Matt Sands and Justin Williams push owners to run their own county research and buy only chain-of-title instruments, but they price the human alternative bluntly: a landman starts around $600 a day, and a limited title search runs about a week and roughly $3,000 [u4xA0UNrxQs @ 00:19:39]. Their newer playbook bolts AI onto the DIY route, feeding deeds into Claude or ChatGPT to build Excel run sheets and compute fractions like 1/12 x 1/160 off a 50-year-old Exhibit A, while warning that early ChatGPT invented case law outright: “Like these cases didn't exist” [NkT15qxxGYM @ 00:10:08]. Dave of titlesearch.com argues from the vendor side that a standard search only walks the surface chain, and that you need a special mineral rights search because the minerals run on a separate chain of title [JpHijIsWFL4 @ 00:01:50]. Money Moves With K sits on the buyer side of the same problem and tells anyone sourcing deals off energynet.com, energydomain.com or county clerk records to run due diligence and a title search to dodge scams [8JwnQSZGjU0 @ 00:04:56]. The operator read: DIY plus AI for the inventory, a paid human or specialty search when the chain itself is in doubt.

Data access splits the camp hardest. Justin Williams calls Oklahoma trickier because it takes more interfaces, and Matt Sands rates the Texas RRC GIS map as the better tool even though the OCC site has improved [GS_N0TTrBPY @ 00:17:04]. North Dakota goes further and walls permits, plats, well files and production behind a Basic subscription at $50 a year, with pooling and spacing orders and hearing audio pushed into an Advanced tier; Matt calls the paywall out directly, saying it is not empowering people to access data that is public information [1HDBzjGoDdc @ 00:19:26]. John Farrell of WellDatabase pitches the counter-model: a free Lite plan with well headers, production, permits, completions and formations, plus paid Essential at $250 a month per user for declines and forecasting, which he says is the only system you could turn on for a month, run the analysis, and turn back off [EDD6HaFdEzE @ 00:30:26]. Farrell's own split: small owners validating checks stay free, while acquirers and anyone facing a buyer upgrade. Steven Hatcher argues the free route is nearly universal, saying most if not all producing states run a similar free GIS system like the Louisiana viewer he demos [5hXDw_OFeQc @ 00:01:49]. Matt himself pays for WellDatabase's paid tier even while sending owners to the free account for North Dakota production.

On the endgame, practitioners do not hand owners one answer. Justin Williams rejects the reflexive family line, “it's not enough to just tell your heirs never sell the minerals,” because heirs may need to sell for medical bills, and he and Matt weigh a trust or LLC against probate while noting a NARO listener named David is running probate himself on small interests [yfXV7bIliEk @ 00:29:00]. Steven Hatcher, who buys minerals as well as practicing oil and gas law, frames his whole channel around teaching valuation so owners can decide to sell or hold in a market he calls incredibly opaque [t1R3KQsH3MQ @ 00:00:52]. The Mineral IQ sponsor read pushes the hold side with an heir who kept the minerals instead of selling at the wrong price [S680WOmo72o @ 00:00:19]. The valuation shortcuts conflict even inside one episode: Matt and Justin give 50 to 60 times average monthly cash flow for wells older than four to five years, then say the rule of thumb is not usable for the IRS, and add lease bonus times 2.5 to 3 only as a floor for undeveloped acreage [u4xA0UNrxQs @ 00:35:33]. Unsolicited offers, both hosts say, land below fair market value. On the Mineral Rights Forum, they warn, you may get four different answers.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest failures are paper failures. Matt Sands and Justin Williams open with heirs who first learn of an inheritance from a landman's phone call, Justin among them, and a NARO member who needed 18 months to untangle an estate from boxes stacked to the ceiling [yfXV7bIliEk @ 00:05:48]. The same episode flags that an unfunded trust still means probate, newly discovered properties must also be deeded into the trust, splitting small interests among four heirs can leave shares worth less than probate, and ancillary probate in another state can be very expensive with attorneys. Once personal representative deeds hit the record, buyers they call vultures start mailing offers. One host's hindsight: “I would absolutely keep everything that might be related to it” [u4xA0UNrxQs @ 00:11:17]. In that same tools episode they recall an attorney who said minerals weren't part of an estate. NARO hammers the point that a royalty statement is a starting point, not a complete ownership record, and that “A check in your name doesn't resolve a gap in the recorded chain of ownership” [o8FqhVu6MNM @ 00:04:48]. Dave of titlesearch.com adds that probate and heirship gaps are common, and that rights can revert to the surface owner if lease terms were breached [JpHijIsWFL4 @ 00:02:29].

Map-reading traps cost real decimals. Justin Williams warns on the Texas RRC walkthrough that a unit can touch your boundary while the first take point sits outside it, so you have to dive into the plat; on horizontal wells only the FTP-to-LTP lateral produces, your share depends on net acres and lateral footage inside your tract, and an allocation-well permit splits production by lateral length [gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:13:20]. In Oklahoma the trap runs the other way: the demo NW/4 of Sec 1-11N-2W has no surface location, yet the Roller 1-36H bottom hole sits in Section 1, an interest an owner scanning only for pads would miss [GS_N0TTrBPY @ 00:04:35]. Matt also warns that a Mineral IQ alert inside a two-mile radius does not prove you own an interest; verify it against the permit and plat. North Dakota adds a dormancy trap: after 20 years unused you must file a statement of claim or lose the minerals to the surface owner [1HDBzjGoDdc @ 00:03:43]. Enverus flags that default spacing settings produce chaotic results and that large coefficient values are often associated with problematic distance results for child wellbores [hYa6oTD7seU @ 00:12:31].

The economics checks carry their own blind spots. On Texas gas, the RRC figure is wet gas while royalty statements show dry gas plus NGLs after shrinkage: “the volume of gas would be less than what's shown on the Railroad Commission website so just keep that in mind” [S680WOmo72o @ 00:28:58]. Texas also reports at the lease level, so you may have to add up wells and read the disposition column, as in April 2012 when 1,990 barrels were produced but 1,905 sold. On AI, Matt and Justin report that it cannot query RRC production data, that websites block AI tools, that free tiers train on your data, and they put it plainly: “don't upload a division order with your social security number on it” [NkT15qxxGYM @ 00:34:48]. John Farrell concedes WellDatabase in-product results are a ballpark, not a full economic analysis, and that large fields need expertise [EDD6HaFdEzE @ 00:29:37]. North Dakota's Basic tier brings friction of its own: a PDF form, email, card payment by phone, and several business days before access [1HDBzjGoDdc @ 00:20:25]. Budget that wait before a production drop forces you to pull the well file.

callout.title: Four checks before you sign, upload or trust a number
callout.body: Each gate comes straight from a loss, near-miss or warning the practitioners hit firsthand while locating and inventorying minerals.
items: Before signing anything, verify which rights the document affects and who the contact actually represents; leasing is not selling [National Association of Royalty Owners — o8FqhVu6MNM @ 00:00:33].
Before trusting an alert or a nearby pad, pull the permit and plat and confirm the first take point and lateral footage fall inside your tract [Matt Sands — gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:13:20].
Never upload a division order carrying your social security number; redact it and run AI only on a paid tier that lets you opt out of training [Matt Sands — NkT15qxxGYM @ 00:34:48].
When a division order arrives, ask the paying company which records and calculations support its decimal before you accept it [National Association of Royalty Owners — o8FqhVu6MNM @ 00:05:38].

Plot the tract on the state GIS viewer, using the Texas RRC Surveys search, and write down the abstract number for faster future searches [Matt Sands — gFgW6n9nb-c @ 00:09:16].

Search county records for free first, then pay only for chain-of-title instruments: mineral, quitclaim and warranty deeds, leases, assignments, ratifications and memoranda [Matt Sands — u4xA0UNrxQs @ 00:12:41].
Build a single spreadsheet holding state, county, legal description, interest type, decimal or net acres, lease status and provenance [Matt Sands — yfXV7bIliEk @ 00:09:57].

chapters.question_prompt: What does my oil and gas lease say, how does it stay alive, and how do pooling and negotiation leverage affect my royalty?
chapters.title: The Oil and Gas Lease, Pooling and Owner Bargaining Power
chapters.subtitle: Granting clause, royalty rate, shut-in and constructive production, cessation, dry-hole and continuous-operations clauses, Pugh clauses, pooling and unitization mechanics, landowner bargaining power, and listener Q&A on lease management
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one rule: the lease is negotiated before signing or not at all. No standard form exists, leases run for decades, and royalty terms outweigh the bonus. Matt Sands prices a fair bonus at mineral value divided by 2 or 3 and calls trading royalty rate for bonus short-sighted, while the Energy Law Professor treats a zero or low bonus as a sign the operator is not serious about drilling. Leverage scales with acreage: Steven Hatcher's 5,000-acre owners command 1/4 cost-free royalties, while 5-acre owners in 1,280-acre units get pooled or excluded. Street mechanics cover tract participation math, 300% force-pool penalties, $300-per-acre deemed leases and Pugh audits. The sharpest split: holding out for better terms versus Hatcher's Haynesville holdouts who lost multi-million-dollar offers.

key_metrics.metric: Fair Lease Bonus Rule of Thumb
key_metrics.value: Mineral value divided by 2 or 3 ($3,000/NMA minerals supports about $1,000/acre bonus)
key_metrics.context: Matt Sands' benchmark for judging a lease bonus offer, given while answering a Nacogdoches County Haynesville offer of $300/NMA on 14.3 net mineral acres.

key_metrics.label: Force-Pooling Risk Penalty
key_metrics.value: 300% ($18M of production on a $6M well before payout)
key_metrics.context: Alice Hog's second election option for a force-pooled owner; reworks reset the penalty, and the default if no election is made is a deemed lease at $300/acre and 1/8.

key_metrics.label: Small-Tract Pooled Royalty Dilution
key_metrics.context: Allocation math showing what a 3/16 royalty owner with 5 acres in a 40-acre pooled unit actually receives.

key_metrics.label: Haynesville Peak Lease Bonus
key_metrics.value: $20,000 per acre across six parishes
key_metrics.context: Steven Hatcher's example of bonus levels during the Haynesville rush, where some holdouts lost multi-million-dollar offers after delineation drilling proved their acreage worthless.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who works lease paper opens with the same warning: there is no standard lease, and the form the landman hands over is a starting point, not a final deal. The Energy Law Professor flags the Producer's 88 as an oil-company-friendly form and points owners toward bank trusts and landowners associations for landowner-friendly paper [WBGDgooXnq8 @ 00:03:11]. Steven Hatcher of Minerals Guy frames the stakes in time, not dollars: a lease can run 20, 30 or 50 years, so the owner's kids may end up living with whatever gets signed, which is why the first pro tip is to refuse to simply sign the landman's form [b97Q2qy5uEo @ 00:02:33]. Tracy Lenz, an engineer reading decades of recorded leases from Utah to Ohio, adds that leases are hard to exit once signed and that no universal standard lease exists across counties or eras [HGUBxgz_6Ak @ 00:01:36]. The professor also notes the one structural edge owners keep after signing: courts read ambiguities against the lessee and imply covenants into the deal [WBGDgooXnq8 @ 00:06:22]. The operator takeaway is blunt. The negotiation happens before the ink dries, because the document then governs royalty, deductions, term and release rights for as long as a well keeps producing in paying quantities.

The second point of agreement is that royalty rate and deduction language matter more than the check at signing. Matt Sands calls trading royalty rate for a bigger bonus 'short-sighted,' because mineral value moves in direct proportion to the royalty rate and that rate sets every future check; the biggest single win, especially in gas plays, is no post-production deduction or marketable-product language [xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:06:37]. Steven Hatcher shows the same split on the page: an 'at the well' royalty lets the operator deduct processing, treating, marketing and transportation, while a cost-free royalty bars gathering, processing and transportation deductions [b97Q2qy5uEo @ 00:10:30]. Tracy Lenz tracks the rate history across recorded leases: 1/8 dominated in the 1980s and earlier, then later paper in McMullen County, Texas reached 25% and a Monroe County, Ohio addendum set 19% over the printed 12.5% [HGUBxgz_6Ak @ 00:06:39]. The Energy Law Professor does not dismiss the bonus entirely, though. A zero or low bonus signals the company is not serious about drilling, and the professor's worked example pairs a $1.5M bonus with a 25% royalty for a $16.5M total to the owner [WBGDgooXnq8 @ 00:22:32]. Consensus: negotiate rate and deductions first, then use the bonus as a seriousness test on the operator.

Practitioners also agree that bargaining power is a function of acreage and the pooling threat. Steven Hatcher splits owners into two classes: a roughly 5,000-acre tract can command a 1/4 gross cost-free royalty, top-of-market bonus, depth severance, a well commitment and possibly a continuous drilling clause, while a 5-acre owner inside a 1,280-acre unit has little leverage because the operator can force pool the tract or simply exclude it [hZZNvuvGfkc @ 00:01:07]. The small owner's move is to benchmark terms against neighbors rather than bluff. Alice Hog of the behoge13 pooling webinar confirms the threat is real almost everywhere: 39 of 50 states have forced pooling, aimed at unleased owners, unlocatable owners and non-participating royalty interest owners, though Texas applies it 'very rarely' [le24nqd0H0M @ 00:28:31]. The Energy Law Professor explains why Texas is different: the Mineral Interest Pooling Act only reaches fields discovered after 1961, and the operator must exhaust voluntary efforts and make 'fair and reasonable offers' before going to the Railroad Commission [W5PjbHVyvWU @ 00:00:59]. The professor adds that fracking flipped the incentives, so drillers are now the ones seeking force pooling [W5PjbHVyvWU @ 00:11:45]. Net result: large tracts dictate terms, small tracts price off the neighborhood.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Execution starts with the recorded instrument. Steven Hatcher's workflow pulls the lease and any assignments from county or parish records, then reads it as who, what, when and how much: lessor and lessee in the first paragraph, where an ancestor in title may appear as lessor, the land in paragraph 2 and possibly Exhibit A, the habendum clause usually in the third paragraph, and the royalty rate under how much. On term math, a lease executed January 1, 2020 with a 3-year primary term expires January 1, 2023 unless held, and paid-up leases carry no rentals [b97Q2qy5uEo @ 00:07:22]. Alex Ottewell's field version: operators typically get about a 3-year window to start drilling, production has to continue monthly, and after 90 days without paying quantities the lease can be lost and the wells must be plugged [VTx53sL4jRk @ 00:00:39]. The savings clauses get read literally. The Energy Law Professor walks through Freeman v. Magnolia, where a late shut-in payment terminated the lease because 'while royalty is so paid' created a condition [7sPTlHr4F7A @ 00:03:56], and Rogers v. Osborne, where a second well failed because the end-of-term sentence lacked the word 'additional,' making it only a well-completion clause [aPa6sCIUG-M @ 00:04:46].

The money math is simple enough to run on a napkin. Matt Sands' bonus rule of thumb: a fair bonus is the mineral value divided by 2 or 3, so minerals worth $3,000 per net mineral acre support a targeted bonus near $1,000 an acre; on a Nacogdoches County Haynesville offer of $300 per NMA across 14.3 net mineral acres, Sands says Mitsubishi's $8B purchase of Aethon's assets will not move bonus rates, and Mitsubishi's capital spending is the real question [xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:06:17]. Alice Hog shows why pooled small tracts disappoint: a 3/16 royalty (.1875) times a 5/40 tract share (.125) yields .0234375, 'really 2% rather than 18%' [le24nqd0H0M @ 00:13:55]. On Texas allocation wells, Sands computes the tract participation factor as productive lateral length divided by total length, first take point to last take point, so 5,000 feet of a 10,000-foot well is one half, then applies net acres in the 640-acre half of a 1,280-acre unit times the royalty rate [5Cx7zTkAJdw @ 00:14:23]. Lengths come off the permit plat and the as-drilled plat at the Railroad Commission, a check that works '99% of the time' [5Cx7zTkAJdw @ 00:17:06].

Two audits separate owners who get paid from owners who get diluted. Michele Johnson of LMJ Land Services runs the Pugh clause check: an acreage Pugh means the unit holds only land inside it, a depth Pugh holds only down to a stated depth, often 100 feet below the deepest producing formation, and 'a lease can be alive and still be much smaller than the lease form says' [sLCs9xQypFE @ 00:00:40]. In the demo, an 80-acre lease on the S/2 SE/4 of Section 59 has only 40 acres in the unit, so the other 40 may no longer be held. The second audit is the force-pooling election. Alice Hog lays out three options: pay a fair share of costs, take a 300% risk penalty under which the operator recovers $18M of production on a $6M well before payout, with reworks resetting it, or accept a deemed lease at $300 per acre and 1/8, which becomes the default if the owner fails to elect [le24nqd0H0M @ 00:35:49]. The Energy Law Professor's Carson case shows where small owners win: an acreage-basis offer made only after drilling on the owner's land, cutting a 1/8 royalty to 1/24, was not fair and reasonable judged from the offeree's standpoint at the time of the offer [W5PjbHVyvWU @ 00:07:12].

callout.title: What the lease paper hides
callout.body: Practitioners repeatedly found the real terms in strike-outs, addenda and clause wording that owners skim past.
items: On a post-1990 lease that shows 1/8, check for strike-outs and addenda; a 1998 Jim Wells County lease had 1/8 struck and replaced with 1/5, and a 2012 Ohio addendum's 19% overrode the printed 12.5% [Tracy Lenz — HGUBxgz_6Ak @ 00:22:21]
A recorded memorandum of lease hides the terms; ask the operator or back-calculate the royalty from 3 of the 4 variables on the check [Tracy Lenz — HGUBxgz_6Ak @ 00:13:01]

Compare competing offers through the Lease Price Report, discounted for NARO members, and the Mineral Rights Forum; county clerk records show royalty rates but a memorandum does not [Matt Sands — xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:09:06]
A 'gas well' or 'gas only' shut-in clause does not cover oil wells or low oil prices: 'If it's actually an oil well, no, you can't shut it in' [Energy Law Professor — 7sPTlHr4F7A @ 00:12:56]

sop_steps.action: Retrieve the lease, assignments and any memorandum from county or parish records.
sop_steps.detail: Leases and their assignments are recorded in county or parish records; read who, what, when and how much, checking Exhibit A for the land description and royalty overrides [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — b97Q2qy5uEo @ 00:03:23]

sop_steps.title: Price the offer
sop_steps.action: Benchmark the bonus at mineral value divided by 2 or 3, then rank royalty rate and deduction language above the bonus.
sop_steps.detail: A $3,000/NMA mineral value targets about a $1,000/acre bonus, and giving up royalty rate for bonus is short-sighted because royalty rate drives every future check [Matt Sands — xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:06:17]

sop_steps.title: Run your unit decimal
sop_steps.action: Convert gross acres to net acres, then apply tract share or tract participation factor and royalty rate.
sop_steps.detail: 160 gross acres at a 50% mineral interest equals 80 net acres; multiply by tract share and royalty to get the decimal the division order should show [behoge13 — le24nqd0H0M @ 00:17:46]

sop_steps.action: Map units and wells against the lease, pull completion depths, and file any force-pool election on time.

sections.title: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split on lease economics is how hard to push bonus versus royalty. Energy Law Professor models a $1.5M bonus stacked on a 25% royalty for a $16.5M landowner take, and flags that a zero or low bonus signals the company is not serious about drilling [WBGDgooXnq8 @ 00:22:32]. Matt Sands comes at it from the other direction: target a bonus of roughly the mineral value divided by 2 or 3, so $3,000 per net mineral acre in value points to about $1,000 an acre in bonus, but never trade royalty rate away to fatten that check [xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:06:17]. Sands calls that swap short-sighted because mineral value moves in direct proportion to the royalty rate, and ranks no post-production deduction, marketable-product language as the biggest single win, especially in gas plays [xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:06:37]. Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy sets the ceiling for big blocks: on roughly 5,000 acres, a 1/4 gross, cost-free royalty is about as good as it gets, paired with top-of-market bonus, depth severance, a well commitment, and possibly a continuous drilling clause [hZZNvuvGfkc @ 00:00:23]. The operator read: bonus is a seriousness signal and a one-time payday, while royalty rate and deduction language compound for the life of the wells.

Leverage depends on tract size, and practitioners disagree on whether holding out pays. Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy says an 800lb gorilla can sit tight and wait for the landman to come back, but a 5-acre owner inside a 1,280-acre unit has little leverage because the operator can force pool the tract or exclude it, so that owner should benchmark terms against neighbors [hZZNvuvGfkc @ 00:01:50]. Energy Law Professor reads Texas law as tilted toward the small owner: in Carson v. Railroad Commission, the Texas Supreme Court judged fairness from the standpoint of the offeree at the time of the offer, favored small tracts, and allowed more than an acreage share [W5PjbHVyvWU @ 00:08:46]. Other states run zoning-like pooling with no small-tract exception, which strips that edge away [W5PjbHVyvWU @ 00:12:47]. Alice Hog of behoge13 counts 39 of 50 states with force pooling, notes Texas applies it very rarely, and flips the leasing math: an unleased owner who stands in as the fourth working-interest owner gets 25% versus 18% as a lessor [le24nqd0H0M @ 00:38:59]. The alternative playbook is to skip the lease entirely, but that only works for an owner who can carry well costs or swallow the penalty that comes with being carried.

Where the royalty is measured is the next fault line. Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy separates at-the-well royalties, which let the lessee deduct processing, treating, marketing, and transportation, from a cost-free royalty that bars gathering, processing, and transportation deductions [b97Q2qy5uEo @ 00:10:30]. Tracy Lenz shows the old-form version in a 1970 Weld County, Colorado lease from Beaver Mesa: 1/8 at the mouth of the well, with post-production costs applied [HGUBxgz_6Ak @ 00:08:05]. Energy Law Professor shows that even the value base splits by state: in a 2001 Texas case the contract price was $8 per mcf, market value was $2, and the landowner got $2; Kansas, Montana, North Dakota, and West Virginia follow that majority rule while Oklahoma's Tara (1981) sits in the minority [dM8LufO_Emg @ 00:16:19]. The same professor maps a parallel split on what holds a lease: Oklahoma lets capability of production hold it so the shut-in payment is for the lessor's benefit, Louisiana keeps it alive pending written notice, and Texas under Stanolind says capability alone does not hold [7sPTlHr4F7A @ 00:09:00]. Read the state and the measuring point together before comparing any two royalty rates.

sections.title: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Termination traps are the costliest failures. Energy Law Professor walks through Freeman v. Magnolia (Texas, 1943), where a late shut-in payment killed the lease because the words 'while royalty is so paid' created a condition, and a 'covenants aren't conditions' clause did not rescue the lessee: 'because the royalty wasn't paid, that condition's not met, the lease expires' [7sPTlHr4F7A @ 00:07:22]. The same professor warns that gas-well or gas-only shut-in language does not cover oil wells or low oil prices: 'If it's actually an oil well, no, you can't shut it in' [7sPTlHr4F7A @ 00:12:56]. In Rogers v. Osborne (Texas 1953), a well that never produced and was not a dry hole fell between both savings clauses, could not carry shut-in royalty because it was not capable of production, and the second well failed because the end-of-term sentence lacked the word 'additional'; the professor adds that courts read these clauses literally and harshly [aPa6sCIUG-M @ 00:04:46]. Alex Ottewell puts the field version bluntly: production must continue monthly, and after 90 days without paying quantities the lease can be lost and the wells must be plugged [VTx53sL4jRk @ 00:00:39]. Check the calendar before the lessee does.

Pooling arithmetic burns owners who read only the royalty fraction. Alice Hog of behoge13 runs it: a 3/16 royalty (.1875) times a 5/40 tract share (.125) yields .0234375, 'really 2% rather than 18%' [le24nqd0H0M @ 00:13:55]. Hog also flags how pooling breaks: in Amoco v. Underwood (1977), carving a sliver of a 2,252-acre lease into a 643-acre unit was bad faith, a lease without a pooling clause does not hold, and when Sunoco pooled for gas and found oil the lease was not held [le24nqd0H0M @ 00:24:00]. The force-pooled owner who sits on the election paper gets the default, a deemed lease at $300 per acre and 1/8, while choosing to be carried means a 300% penalty, $18M of production on a $6M well before payout, with reworks resetting the clock [le24nqd0H0M @ 00:37:31]. Michele Johnson of LMJ Land Services catches the reverse trap in acquisitions: a Pugh clause limits what a well or unit can hold, so lease three covering the S/2 SE/4 of Section 59, 80 acres, may keep only the 40 acres inside the unit, because 'a lease can be alive and still be much smaller than the lease form says' [sLCs9xQypFE @ 00:00:40]. Buyers assuming the whole lease is held are pricing acreage that may already be released.

Paper traps and outright scams round out the failures. Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy warns against just signing the landman's form because leases can run 20, 30, or 50 years and your kids may live with the document [b97Q2qy5uEo @ 00:02:33]. Tracy Lenz shows why the paper matters: a 1999 memorandum of lease hides the terms, a 2012 Monroe County, Ohio addendum at 19% overrides the printed 12.5%, and any post-1990 lease showing 1/8 needs a check for strike-outs and addenda [HGUBxgz_6Ak @ 00:22:21]. Matt Sands fields a caller whose number traced to a hospital and warns of fake term royalty deeds that convey all future royalties just before wells are drilled, at cents on the dollar, such as $3,000 offered against $50 a year in checks: 'if it seems too good to be true, it probably is' [xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:12:49]. On the operator side, Sands describes a landman fraud case where the operator kept title to elderly investors' interests and paid only distribution reports; the fix was a litigator rather than a general oil and gas attorney, often on contingency at a 30% cut of recovered damages, with 'trust but verify' as the standing rule [5Cx7zTkAJdw @ 00:11:11]. Every one of these losses started with paper nobody pulled and read.

Reading the royalty fraction as the actual pooled payout
3/16 times 5/40 equals .0234375, really 2% rather than 18% of production
Multiply royalty rate by tract share before valuing any pooled interest
behoge13 ([le24nqd0H0M @ 00:13:55])
Ignoring the force-pooling election deadline entirely

callout.title: Four checks before the lease, the election, or the sale
callout.body: Each gate below maps to a loss a practitioner watched happen: a lease expiring on a late payment, a pooled decimal far below the headline fraction, a default election, and a cents-on-the-dollar deed.
items: Confirm every shut-in royalty payment lands on time, because a late payment under 'while royalty is so paid' language terminated the lease in Freeman v. Magnolia [Energy Law Professor — 7sPTlHr4F7A @ 00:07:22].
Run royalty rate times tract share before valuing a pooled interest; 3/16 on a 5/40 tract is really 2% rather than 18% [behoge13 — le24nqd0H0M @ 00:13:55].
Make the force-pooling election in writing before the deadline, or default into a deemed lease at $300 per acre and 1/8 [behoge13 — le24nqd0H0M @ 00:37:31].

Pull deeds, leases, and assignments before answering any unsolicited term royalty deed offer, since these convey all future royalties just before drilling at cents on the dollar [Matt Sands — xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:12:49].

chapters.pull_quote: "So, a lease can be alive and still be much smaller than the lease form says." Michele Johnson, LMJ Land Services (sLCs9xQypFE @ 00:00:40).
action_checklist: Pull the base lease and every recorded assignment from county or parish records, then read the granting, habendum, and royalty paragraphs before signing anything [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — b97Q2qy5uEo @ 00:03:23].
Set the target bonus at mineral value divided by 2 or 3 and refuse to trade royalty rate for a bigger bonus check [Matt Sands — xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:06:17].

Benchmark the offer against the Lease Price Report, the Mineral Rights Forum, and county clerk records, knowing a recorded memorandum of lease will not show the royalty rate [Matt Sands — xiP5PiaaYKE @ 00:09:06].

Verify an allocation-well decimal by dividing your productive lateral length by total length, first take point to last take point, using the permit plat and as-drilled plat [Matt Sands — 5Cx7zTkAJdw @ 00:17:06].
Build a Pugh column on the lease schedule: read every word of the clause, find its effective date, map units and wells, and pull completion depths [LMJ Land Services — sLCs9xQypFE @ 00:00:40].
When force pooled, choose between paying a fair share of costs, a 300% carried penalty, or the deemed lease before the default election kicks in [behoge13 — le24nqd0H0M @ 00:35:49].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I calculate working interest and net revenue interest for owners, co-tenants and operators, including in pooled units?
chapters.title: Working the Numbers: WI and NRI Calculations
chapters.subtitle: Three-step NRI calculation, gross working interest, operator NRI after royalties and overrides, AAPL study-guide situations with NPRIs, pooled-unit acreage problems, and undivided co-tenant interests with different royalties
chapters.executive_summary: Landmen and mineral owners working these numbers agree on one spine: before a lease the mineral owner holds 100% working interest and 100% net revenue interest; after the lease the lessee takes 100% of the WI and the lessor keeps only the royalty fraction. From there every division-order decimal is built by multiplication: royalty times mineral interest times tract acres over unit acres. Matt Sands turns 16 net acres in a 1,280-acre DSU at a 15% royalty into .001875 and a roughly $937 three-month check estimate. Alyce Hoge and the Land Training drills show 1/8 leaving the operator 0.875 and 3/16 leaving 0.8125, with overrides and NPRIs carved out further. UHD's instructor insists on a lease-level check-and-balance, while Land Training leans on Excel fill-down and summing back to the tract share.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The cleanest consensus across the Land Training sessions and Alyce Hoge's lease breakdown is the grand bargain. Before any oil and gas lease, the mineral owner holds 100% of the working interest and 100% of the net revenue interest, meaning they pay every drilling bill and keep every barrel, while the oil company owns 0% of both. Sign the lease and the lessor hands 100% of the working interest to the lessee, keeping only a royalty fraction in return [eZU5hvGcngg @ 00:03:47]. The Land Training instructor runs the same trade through the Harry Truman fact pattern: Hiroshima Drilling leases all 160 acres for a 1/8 royalty, leaving Truman with 0% working interest and a 0.125 net revenue interest, while the company holds 100% working interest and a 0.875 net revenue interest [PjGnR-YfLy4 @ 00:07:07]. Why would an owner accept that split? Every speaker answers with risk. Hoge prices a well at about $6 million and stresses that a dry hole is the company's loss alone; the royalty owner pays nothing [eZU5hvGcngg @ 00:05:34]. A second Land Training walkthrough puts the cost at a million dollars and up, climbing with every rework, and calls drilling cost prohibitive for most landowners [yWZaJ-ItXKQ @ 00:02:51]. The lessor trades cost exposure for a clean, cost-free slice of production.

The second point of agreement is that pooling shrinks the royalty by acreage, and everyone uses the same multiplication. The Land Training instructor explains that state conservation agencies, the Texas Railroad Commission, Louisiana's Department of Conservation and the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, cap wells per acreage, so owners without a wellbore on their tract still share production in proportion to the acres they contribute [WPeA0rs7SLA @ 00:04:17]. The formula: royalty interest times tract acres divided by unit acres. Hoge runs a lessor with 160 acres in a 640-acre gas unit at 3/16 and lands on 0.046875, warning that these decimals usually run out to eight decimal places [eZU5hvGcngg @ 00:13:51]. Matt Sands, coming at it from the mineral owner's chair, builds the identical equation from three inputs that take under five minutes once gathered: net mineral acres, drilling spacing unit size and lease royalty rate [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:01:35]. Another Land Training walkthrough lands on 1/32, or 0.03125, for 160 of 640 acres at 1/8 [yWZaJ-ItXKQ @ 00:09:51]. Practitioners also agree on where the numbers live: working interest on the joint interest billing deck, net revenue interest on the division order pay sheet. If the operator's decimal disagrees with the owner's math, the owner digs in.

Third, the operator's net revenue interest is always gross working interest minus burdens, and overrides come off the company's side, never the lessor's. The UHD instructor calls net revenue interest the most important number an oil company has, the take-home pay after deductions, and lays out the order: calculate gross working interest first, calculate every burden second, then subtract [oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:00:36]. The Land Training instructor applies it to Adam's 1/8 lease with a 3% override assigned to the geologist: the override is carved out of the working interest, so the company's 0.875 drops to 0.845 and the geologist holds a 0.03 decimal that pays nothing if the well is dry [B5fBIyi1-hw @ 00:04:40]. Non-participating royalties hit the other side of the ledger. When Alpha conveys 2.5% of the oil and gas produced and saved to Bravo and then leases to Charlie at 1/8, Alpha's 12.5% shrinks to 10%, Bravo keeps 2.5%, and Charlie still holds 87.5% [JVbDAxk_YTU @ 00:04:49]. The instructor flags 'produced and saved' as the buzzwords that separate a royalty conveyance from a mineral conveyance, and notes that nobody takes a lease from the NPRI holder [HkEK5QVZAJ0 @ 00:01:14]. Whoever granted the burden absorbs it: the lessee for the override, the mineral owner for the NPRI.
