sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Matt Sands teaches the owner-side workflow as three inputs and one equation. Net mineral acres come from the legal description: gross acres times decimal ownership, so a 1/40 interest, 2.5%, in a 640-acre section yields 16 net mineral acres; if the decimal is unknown, a landman or lawyer's title search running the chain of transfers in county records supplies it [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:06:19]. Drilling spacing unit size comes off the state oil and gas commission's map; in North Dakota, Sands uses the Industrial Commission's GIS map server, turns on the spacing-unit layer, finds the section and reads a 1,280-acre, two-section DSU for a horizontal Bakken well. The royalty rate sits on page one of the lease, in the clause delivering the lessor's share free of cost into the tanks or pipeline, here 15%, pulled from the county clerk and recorder if the owner has no copy [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:10:11]. Then 16 divided by 1,280 times 0.15 equals .001875, the decimal that must match the division order [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:12:22]. Alyce Hoge confirms operators build the same figure, net acres over unit acres times the royalty fraction, which is how those crazy eight-place decimals appear on the pay deck [eZU5hvGcngg @ 00:12:21].

Once ownership splits, the formula gains a factor. The Land Training instructor's spacing-unit formula for co-tenants is royalty interest times mineral interest times tract acres divided by unit acres, and they keep mineral interest as its own term so errors stay traceable [wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:04:21]. The lease itself only shows 160 acres; the actual mineral interest comes from the lease purchase report built off the landman's chain of title, so assuming 100% from the lease face is wrong. In the Brady heirs problem, four children each hold 25% undivided in 160 acres inside a 320-acre unit: Greg at 1/4 royalty nets 0.03125, Peter at 3/16 nets 0.0234375, and Bobby and Cindy at 1/8 net 0.015625 each. The instructor builds it in Excel, typing the formula once with an equals sign, then dragging the fill handle when the skinny plus sign appears to populate every row [wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:10:21]. The single-owner drills stay fast: Franklin Roosevelt's 20 acres in an 80-acre unit at 3/16 come to 0.046875 [kw0rYmoBLXU @ 00:01:34], while Budro's 160 acres in a 160-acre unit keep the full 0.1875 because the tract fills the unit. Ten Marcellus acres at 1/5 in an 80-acre unit work out to 0.20 times 10 over 80, or 0.025 [kC2dYFP0U0g @ 00:01:04].

Burdens get the same discipline. The UHD instructor's Sunrise Oil and Gas example: 100% gross working interest in Homer Murray's 80-acre lease, 12.5% royalty, 5% override to the geologist, so Sunrise pockets 82.5 cents on every dollar [oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:05:22]. Pool the 80 acres into a 320-acre unit and Sunrise's unit gross becomes 0.25, Homer's unit royalty 0.03125, the override 0.0125, because it is tied to Homer's acres, leaving a 0.20625 net. The check: 0.825 times 0.25 must equal 0.20625, and it does [oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:09:36]. The UHD instructor's caution: if Sunrise brings five leases with different burdens, run the check lease by lease, never commingled, or the totals will not reconcile. Always run it, the instructor says, even when you think you aced the math. Land Training checks the co-tenant split the same way, summing royalty and lessee shares back to each owner's mineral interest times the unit factor, as with Greg's 0.5 times 0.25 equaling 0.125 [n2pg2-Q06P8 @ 00:10:23]. On paper, the landman writes the full fraction, 1/8, 3/16 or 1/6, into each co-tenant's lease, never the reduced decimal; the proportionate reduction clause then lets the division order drop Greg's 1/8 to 0.0625 based on what Greg actually owns [PNLVi6Ee0KM @ 00:09:16].

callout.title: Shortcuts and tells the practitioners lean on
callout.body: Small habits that keep a division-order decimal honest before anyone signs or cashes a check.
items: Watch for 'produced and saved' in any conveyance: it signals a royalty, not minerals, so the grantee is an NPRI holder and the mineral owner's NRI shrinks once a lease is signed [Land Training www.landtraining.net — JVbDAxk_YTU @ 00:01:03].

Do not answer 9.5% when no lease exists yet: David simply owns 100% of the minerals subject to Charlie's 3% NPRI until a lease royalty is set [Land Training www.landtraining.net — HkEK5QVZAJ0 @ 00:04:30].

Expect the realized price to trail the benchmark: Sands cites WTI at $60 while Bakken barrels bring $50 because of the price differential for transport and processing, and state production data can lag a couple of months [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:16:47].

Keep mineral interest as its own column in Excel instead of folding it into the acres, so a bad input is visible and traceable when the decimal looks off [Land Training www.landtraining.net — wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:04:43].

sop_steps.title: Pin down net mineral acres and true mineral interest
sop_steps.action: Multiply gross tract acres by the decimal ownership from the legal description or title work.
sop_steps.detail: Sands gets 16 net mineral acres from 2.5% of 640 acres and falls back on a landman's title search when the decimal is unknown [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:06:19]; lease administration confirms the actual mineral interest on the lease purchase report, not the lease face [Land Training www.landtraining.net — wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:02:40].

sop_steps.title: Pull unit size and the lease royalty rate
sop_steps.action: Read the DSU from the state commission GIS layer and the royalty from page one of the lease.
sop_steps.detail: Sands turns on the spacing-unit layer on the North Dakota map server, reads a 1,280-acre DSU, and takes the 15% royalty from the delivery clause, pulling the lease from the county clerk and recorder if needed [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:10:11].

sop_steps.title: Run the formula, then subtract operator burdens
sop_steps.action: Multiply royalty x mineral interest x tract acres / unit acres; for the lessee, subtract every burden from gross WI.
sop_steps.detail: The co-tenant formula stacks royalty, mineral interest and tract-over-unit acres [Land Training www.landtraining.net — wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:00:42]; the operator's 0.875 less a 0.03 override leaves 0.845 [Land Training www.landtraining.net — B5fBIyi1-hw @ 00:05:21].

sop_steps.title: Check, reconcile and challenge
sop_steps.action: Run a check-and-balance per lease, compare to the division order, and challenge mismatches.
sop_steps.detail: UHD checks 0.825 x 0.25 against the 0.20625 net and runs each lease separately when burdens differ [UHD Continuing and Professional Education — oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:10:00]; Sands goes back to the operator who sent the division order when a verified calculation does not match [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:12:07].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Matt Sands and the Land Training instructors reach the same decimal through different keystrokes, and the order matters when you hunt for an error. Sands front-loads the ownership fraction: multiply gross acreage by your decimal interest to get net mineral acres, so 2.5% of a 640-acre section yields 16 NMA, then divide by the 1280-acre DSU and multiply by the 15% royalty to land on .001875 [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:06:19]. The Land Training co-tenant playbook refuses to pre-blend: royalty interest times mineral interest times tract acres divided by unit acres. The instructor explains that keeping the mineral interest as its own factor 'helps you know if there's a mistake where you can go back and look at it' [wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:04:43]. For a 100% owner, the pooled-unit drills strip the formula down to royalty times tract acres over unit acres. Problem 2 shows that a 160-acre tract in a 160-acre spacing unit leaves Boudreaux's 3/16 royalty untouched at .1875 [VPrc0ax0-_o @ 00:01:26]. The operator takeaway is a split by use case. Sands's collapsed NMA method is faster for a single mineral owner reading one division order. The separated-factor method scales better when four heirs, three royalty rates, and one spacing unit all hit the same pay deck and you need to isolate which input broke the number.

Sands pitches self-service. With net mineral acres, DSU size, and royalty rate in hand, the math 'should take you less than five minutes,' and the county clerk and recorder website is 'worth giving it a shot yourself first' before paying a landman to pull the lease [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:09:40]. Sands flips that advice for bigger positions. When multiple horizontal wells are being drilled, Sands recommends a petroleum engineer for reserves and a proper production forecast, plus a landman, because you 'could actually own more or less' than you think [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:18:14]. The Land Training instructor routes the grind into Excel instead. After fumbling a hand calculation on Bobby's interest, the instructor says 'this is why we want to use a spreadsheet,' builds royalty, mineral, tract, and unit columns, and drags the formula down to fill every heir's row [wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:08:19]. The UHD instructor adds a verification layer that the other two playbooks do not mandate: 'always do a check and a balance even if it feels cumbersome.' The check multiplies the lease-level take of 82.5 cents on the dollar by the unit gross working interest of 0.25 and confirms it matches the gross-minus-burdens figure of .20625 [oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:08:28]. That gives an operator three playbooks at three cost levels: free solo math, spreadsheet automation, or hired professionals.

The practitioners also split on whose pocket a burden comes out of, and the answer changes every decimal downstream. An overriding royalty rides on the operator. In Situation #3, the oil company assigns a 3% override to its geologist, and that override is 'carved out of the working interest.' The company's 0.875 drops to a 0.845 net revenue interest, while Adam's .125 royalty stays whole [B5fBIyi1-hw @ 00:02:56]. A non-participating royalty rides on the mineral owner instead. In Situation #4, Alpha conveys 2.5% of the oil and gas produced and saved to Bravo, then leases to Charlie at 1/8. Alpha's 12.5% shrinks to a 10% net revenue interest, while Charlie the lessee keeps the full 87.5% [JVbDAxk_YTU @ 00:03:42]. On the company side, the royalty fraction itself is the lever, and Alyce Hoge walks it down the board. A 1/8 royalty leaves the operator 87.5%, 3/16 leaves 81.25%, and a quarter royalty leaves 75%, because the company's net revenue interest 'decreases the higher the royalty goes' [eZU5hvGcngg @ 00:10:32]. Read the conveyance language before touching a calculator. Situation #4 teaches that 'produced and saved' signals a royalty conveyance rather than minerals, and that one phrase decides which party's decimal absorbs the hit [JVbDAxk_YTU @ 00:01:03].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first failure mode is feeding the formula a bad input. The Land Training instructor warns that a lease reading 160 acres never states the lessor's fractional ownership. In the instructor's words, 'if you look at just the lease and it says 160 Acres you might assume that Greg owns 100, that would be incorrect,' so lease administration has to pull the lease purchase report [wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:02:40]. Sands flags a timing trap on production data. State commission sites update monthly and 'may lag a couple of months,' so a May lookup may only surface February or March volumes, and a brand-new well may not show at all [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:13:41]. Price is the next leak. Sands notes that Bakken barrels can clear at 50 dollars when WTI prints 60, because of a price differential tied to transport and processing costs, and that operator hedging blurs the average price on the check stub further [Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:16:47]. The AAPL study-guide trap is premature math. In Situation #5, a 1/8 lease minus Charlie's 3% NPRI would net David 9.5%, but no lease exists yet. The instructor says 'don't be thinking the answer to this is 9.5%,' because the correct answer is 100% minerals subject to the 3% NPRI [HkEK5QVZAJ0 @ 00:04:30]. Each of these errors produces a clean-looking decimal that is simply wrong.

The second failure mode is fat-fingering decimals, and the instructors commit it live on camera. While checking the four Brady heirs' joint-ownership total, the Land Training instructor stalls mid-multiplication with 'oh I did that wrong sorry.' It takes a third pass before 0.03125 times four reconciles back to the original 1/8 royalty [pjP04Ns4pww @ 00:06:07]. In Pooled Unit Problem 4, a one-fifth royalty on 10 acres inside an 80-acre Marcellus drilling and spacing unit correctly computes to 0.025. It then gets restated aloud as 'a 0.25 is the net revenue interest,' a tenfold slip that would wreck a pay deck if it reached a division order [kC2dYFP0U0g @ 00:01:26]. In the unit co-tenant lesson, the calculator returns 014063 for Peter's royalty share in the 640-acre unit, and the whiteboard receives 01463, a dropped zero that silently shifts the figure [n2pg2-Q06P8 @ 00:06:59]. Alyce Hoge explains why slips like these hide so well. Division order decimals 'usually go out to eight decimal places,' which is how owners end up staring at 'crazy decimals' they cannot eyeball [eZU5hvGcngg @ 00:13:51]. The practitioner fix is structural: separate factor columns, Excel formulas copied down the sheet, and a closing sum that must reconcile.

The third failure mode is running a check that cannot catch the error. The UHD instructor's paycheck analogy is blunt: if the payroll person botches a deduction, take-home pay is wrong. Likewise, 'if we make a mistake anywhere before we get to the net it will affect the net revenue interest' [oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:04:15]. The same instructor caps the method with a warning. When an operator brings five leases with different burdens into one unit, 'you can't co-mingle them.' The check has to run lease by lease, or it will not return the gross-minus-burdens figure [oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:10:21]. The unit co-tenant lesson supplies a per-owner reconciliation. Greg's royalty share plus the lessee's share must sum to 0.125, which equals his 0.5 mineral interest times the 0.25 unit factor, and the same test holds for Peter and Bobby [n2pg2-Q06P8 @ 00:10:23]. On the paper side, the Land Training instructor warns lease drafters not to write 0.0625 into a lease for a 50% owner. Write 1/8 instead and let the proportionate reduction clause cut the royalty on the division order, because that clause is what gives the operator the right to reduce it [PNLVi6Ee0KM @ 00:09:16]. Skip the clause logic, and the lease and the pay deck stop agreeing.

callout.title: Do not release a decimal to the pay deck until these four clear
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a mistake or warning a practitioner reported while working live WI and NRI numbers.
items: Recompute every division order decimal from NMA, DSU acres, and royalty rate, and challenge the operator if your number does not match [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:12:22].
Never take mineral interest from the face of the lease; confirm it on the lease purchase report [Land Training www.landtraining.net — wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:02:40].
Run the check and balance lease by lease when an operator brings multiple leases with different burdens into a unit [UHD Continuing and Professional Education — oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:10:21].

Write the full royalty fraction in the lease and let the proportionate reduction clause produce the reduced decimal on the division order [Land Training www.landtraining.net — PNLVi6Ee0KM @ 00:09:16].

chapters.pull_quote: Always do a check and a balance even if it feels cumbersome, even if it feels like you hardly ever make a mistake. Attributed to UHD Continuing and Professional Education (oHKF06pFkh0 @ 00:08:28).
action_checklist: Multiply gross tract acreage by your decimal interest to get net mineral acres, and order a title search if the decimal is unknown [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:06:19].
Pull the drilling spacing unit size from the state oil and gas commission GIS map by turning on the DSU layer for your section [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:07:46].
Read the royalty clause on the first page of the lease and convert fractions like 1/8 or 1/5 to decimals [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:10:11].
Build an Excel sheet with royalty, mineral interest, tract acres, and unit acres columns, then drag the formula down every owner row [Land Training www.landtraining.net — wUqopw4hh2o @ 00:10:21].
Subtract any override from the operator's 0.875 before reporting its NRI, as in 0.875 minus 0.03 equals 0.845 [Land Training www.landtraining.net — B5fBIyi1-hw @ 00:05:00].

Estimate the royalty check as barrels times price times NRI, as in 10,000 barrels times 50 dollars times .001875 equals about 937 dollars, and dig deeper if the actual check differs significantly [Matt Sands — Yy7az5T7_vs @ 00:15:38].

chapters.question_prompt: What is a division order, should I sign it, and how do I verify the decimal interest on my royalty check?
chapters.title: Division Orders and the Decimal Interest on Your Check
chapters.subtitle: What division orders may contain and what you can strike (Texas and Oklahoma), checking the decimal before signing, converting royalty fractions to decimals, the money decimal, and barrel-to-check royalty math
chapters.executive_summary: Mineral-rights practitioners treat the division order as the operator's statement of your decimal interest, not a lease amendment, and agree that the decimal gets rebuilt before anything is signed: net mineral acres divided by unit acres times lease royalty rate. Matt Sands runs 160/1280 x 18.75% to 0.0234375; Royalty Clerk, NARO, Steven Hatcher and Mineral View run parallel checks and tell owners to demand the operator's working in writing when numbers diverge. The W-9 goes back no matter what to dodge roughly 28% backup withholding. The split is over the paper itself: Blue Mesa Minerals swaps in the NADOA model form, which nearly all of about 130 operators accept, while Oklahoma attorney Richard Winblad says never sign even that form, citing Hull v. Sun Refining, attorney fees, and 12% compounded interest on late pay.

key_metrics.label: Pooled-Unit Decimal Benchmark
key_metrics.value: 0.0234375 (160 net mineral acres / 1,280-acre unit x 18.75% royalty)
key_metrics.context: Worked example of the exact number that should appear on the division order for every well in a two-section horizontal spacing unit under a 3/16 lease.

key_metrics.label: Cost of a Half-Size Decimal
key_metrics.value: $781.25 per month, $9,375 per year, $187,500 over 20 years
key_metrics.context: On a well generating $100,000 a month, the gap between a correct 0.015625 decimal and an order showing 0.0078125, in a simplified 20-year illustration.

key_metrics.label: NADOA Model Form Acceptance Rate
key_metrics.value: Problems with maybe 2 of about 130 operators
key_metrics.context: Firsthand record of substituting the NADOA model division order for operator forms carrying objectionable language such as cost-deduction terms.

key_metrics.label: Oklahoma Late-Payment Interest
key_metrics.value: 12 percent, compounded annually
key_metrics.context: Interest owed under Oklahoma law when royalty payments are not made timely, including when an operator withholds over an unreturned division order.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus — The Decimal Is the Document
paragraphs: Every practitioner on the circuit frames the division order the same way: it is the operator's written claim about what you own in a specific well, sent so you can confirm or contest it before the money starts moving. Matt Sands and co-host Justin Williams describe it as a legal instrument documenting your interest and the products sold, carrying your decimal, the effective date of production, payment timing and minimum payment amounts, and stress that it is not a modification of your lease terms [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:02:13]. Steven Hatcher, an oil and gas attorney who has also run an operator's land department, walks through the pipeline behind it: landmen lease the unit, a title attorney reviews mineral title before drilling, then a division order title opinion lists every lessor, lessee and working interest owner, and division order analysts build the pay deck that must add up to 100 percent [Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:03:04]. NARO adds that the order issues after first production and ties directly to the numbers on your check stub [W3POOsq6ka0 @ 00:00:05]. The triggers are consistent across speakers: a new well, a change of ownership through inheritance or sale, or a change of operator, each of which spawns a fresh order to re-execute [SfX6ycoYg24 @ 00:00:56].

The second point of total agreement is that the decimal is the one number worth fighting over, and that owners can rebuild it themselves with three inputs. NARO's version: know the state-set spacing unit, your net mineral acres inside that unit, and the royalty you negotiated; a 640-acre unit, 80 acres and a 3/16 lease yields 0.0234375, and if that figure is missing from the order, call the division order department and tell them they made a mistake or convince you otherwise [W3POOsq6ka0 @ 00:02:47]. Steven Hatcher runs 40 net acres at a 20 percent royalty in a 640-acre unit to 0.0125, then reverses the math, multiplying the order's decimal by unit size and dividing by royalty rate, to expose how many acres the operator actually credited you with [Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:05:44]. Royalty Clerk calls it the one number on the order that moves every check and rebuilds 1/4 times 5 acres over 1,280 to 0.0097656 [DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:02:56]. The UHD land curriculum stacks a fourth factor for fractional title: 160 acres in a 640-acre pool, 50 percent mineral ownership under the proportionate reduction clause, and a 1/8 royalty produce a 0.015625 share of all production from the well [QKj_eILAG2k @ 00:11:33].

Consensus also holds on the housekeeping that protects cash flow. Whatever you decide about signing, the W-9 goes back: NARO says skip it and the operator must withhold 28 percent of your royalty income for the IRS [W3POOsq6ka0 @ 00:01:31], and Matt Sands prefers taking the full payment and setting aside estimated tax money personally rather than waiting on a refund [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:09:27]. Speakers also agree the analyst on the other side is usually a partner, not an adversary. Hatcher, from both sides of the desk, says the division order analyst and landman want to pay everyone correctly but mistakes do happen, so the first move on a bad number is a call to the operator's land department [Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:08:45]. Sands and Williams add that title opinions behind these orders are very thorough, so most orders are accurate, yet the owner still has to check: the first check after the order is entered should match the decimal, and each later stub should be compared against the order and against prior stubs, with an annual reconciliation to the 1099 [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:36:49]. The same speakers insist on keeping the lease, the offer letter showing net acres, and every executed order on file.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Matt Sands teaches the decimal check as a three-step drill built on paperwork most owners already hold. Step one: dust off the lease offer letter, which states your net mineral acres; an undivided one-quarter interest in a 640-acre section is 160 net mineral acres, leased in the example at $1,000 per acre and a 3/16 royalty [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:13:18]. Step two: pull the plat and permit from the state oil and gas commission site, or the spacing and pooling orders, to get the drilling spacing unit, here 1,280 acres across two sections. Step three: 160 divided by 1,280 times 18.75 percent equals 0.0234375, the number that should appear on the order for every well in that unit [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:15:50]. Co-host Justin Williams lists the toolkit: commission websites for spacing data, county clerk and recorder offices for ownership, Mineral IQ or a well database, and Sands's free net revenue interest spreadsheet, with a landman or oil and gas attorney when records are thin [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:17:14]. Inherited interests with no offer letter force a full title search from patent forward. Royalty Clerk's script closes the loop: ask how the payer calculated the decimal and request the net mineral acres and unit acres it used [DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:04:18].

The base formula breaks in predictable places, and practitioners name each one. In Oklahoma, a Blanchard interest splits the royalty into the 1/8 statutory minimum plus a Blanchard slice, so a 3/16 lease shows as 1/8 plus 1/16 that the owner must add together; owning several tracts in one pooled unit likewise produces separate line items per tract that sum to the real total [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:22:12]. Texas allocation and production sharing wells pay on lateral length through your tract; Steven Hatcher's shortcut is to take the unit decimal and multiply by the share of wellbore in your unit, so 50 percent of the lateral halves it [Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:06:37]. Richard Winblad adds that for Oklahoma horizontals you need the percentage of perforations within your section from the survey [iD4uCjptCXM @ 00:06:27]. On precision, Sands notes orders run to the eighth decimal place, irregular lots such as 39.08 acres instead of 40 cause small mismatches, and an error in that last digit costs one penny per million dollars of revenue, so chasing it can burn hundreds or thousands of dollars to recover cents [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:29:18]. Royalty Clerk draws the same line: an eighth-digit mistake does not matter, a fourth-digit mistake does.

The dollar stakes justify the drill. Mineral View models a well grossing $100,000 a month: a correct 0.015625 decimal is worth $1,562.50 before taxes and deductions, while an order showing roughly half, 0.0078125, pays about $781.25, a gap of $9,375 a year and $187,500 over a simplified 20-year illustration [KYu7M4t5LAk @ 00:02:08]. Royalty Clerk shows how small errors compound: on 10,000 barrels at $70, the right 0.0097656 decimal pays $683.59, but a decimal 2.7 percent low pays $665, leaving the owner $18.59 short every month on oil alone [blbomhUd0sA @ 00:02:22]. Payment timing is the other negotiable lever. Sands says Oklahoma owners can elect a $25 minimum threshold so small or declining wells keep producing regular checks instead of one annual payment once a $100 threshold is hit [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:03:59]. Richard Winblad goes further, saying Oklahoma owners with proceeds between $25 and $100 can request monthly payment. Royalty Clerk lays out the Texas clock: first payment from a new well within 120 days after the end of the month of first sale, then oil within 60 days and gas within 90, late-pay interest at two points above the New York Fed lending rate, and once-a-year payment allowed when $100 or less is owed [SAMqfyu0Ovo @ 00:05:23].

callout.title: Shortcuts the Pros Use on the Decimal
callout.body: Fast moves that surface a wrong decimal or a bad clause before the order goes back in the mail.
items: When your number misses, ask the operator for the one or two redacted title opinion pages that mention your interest; Sands says operators sometimes share them and they show exactly how the decimal was built [Matt Sands — tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:24:58].

Run the math backward: if the reverse calculation credits you with 20 acres instead of 40, call the operator's land department and work it out before signing [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:08:30].

On a Texas order, strike every clause beyond the statutory list, initial each strike with a line saying you do not agree, and return it by a method that gives proof of delivery [Royalty Clerk — DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:03:58].

Hold the stub's decimal against the lease fraction: an old 1/8 number pays exactly half of a 1/4 royalty, so a stub showing the 1/8 figure on a 1/4 lease means you are paid half [Royalty Clerk — blbomhUd0sA @ 00:01:11].

sop_steps.title: Assemble the three inputs
sop_steps.action: Pull the lease or offer letter for net mineral acres and royalty rate, then the plat, permit, or pooling order for unit size.
sop_steps.detail: Go to the state oil and gas commission website for the plat and permit showing the drilling spacing unit, and use the lease packet letter for net mineral acres [Matt Sands — tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:14:16].

sop_steps.title: Rebuild and reverse the decimal
sop_steps.action: Compute net mineral acres over unit acres times royalty, then multiply the order's decimal by unit size and divide by royalty rate.
sop_steps.detail: The reverse calculation reveals the acres the operator credited you with, such as 0.0125 x 640 / 0.20 = 40 acres [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:05:44].

sop_steps.title: Scrub the language
sop_steps.action: Compare every clause to the NADOA model form and strike indemnity, warranty-of-title, or cost-deduction terms that conflict with your lease.
sop_steps.detail: Transfer the property and owner information onto the NADOA model form and submit it in place of the operator's order when objectionable language appears [Blue Mesa Minerals — SfX6ycoYg24 @ 00:06:06].

sop_steps.title: Return the paper and audit the first check
sop_steps.action: Send the W-9 with your response, then match the first royalty check's decimal to the division order.
sop_steps.detail: The W-9 blocks 28 percent backup withholding [NARO — W3POOsq6ka0 @ 00:01:31], and the first check after the analyst enters the order should carry the same decimal or it is time to raise concern [Matt Sands — tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:36:49].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over the NADOA model form. Blue Mesa Minerals treats it as the default swap: copy the well name, owner number and decimal off the operator's paper onto the model form and mail that back instead, reporting roughly 130 operators handled and trouble with maybe two of them [SfX6ycoYg24 @ 00:06:26]. When an operator's own form already mirrors model-form language, Blue Mesa returns it; the swap is reserved for paper carrying 'interesting language.' Matt Sands runs a softer version, using the NADOA form as a redline benchmark so only model-form language survives on anything Sands signs, and crossing out clauses that drag in liability such as warranty of title [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:05:00]. Richard Winblad, an Oklahoma attorney practicing since 1992, says the model form is not okay for Oklahoma wells. Winblad's objections: it makes you certify a decimal you lack the title opinion and training to verify, it makes you indemnify and reimburse the payer for its own overpayment mistakes, and it accepts a $100 minimum pay when Oklahoma law lets owners request monthly checks on proceeds between $25 and $100 [iD4uCjptCXM @ 00:04:43]. The replacement packet is a W-9, a letter citing the statute and Hull v. Sun Refining, a bare-bones information form, and a statement about interest due for nonpayment [iD4uCjptCXM @ 00:09:16].

Whether you must sign at all splits by state. NARO and Blue Mesa both say Texas requires a signed division order before you enter pay status, while Oklahoma does not [W3POOsq6ka0 @ 00:01:00]. Royalty Clerk narrows the Texas rule: a payer may demand a signature only on seven listed items, from effective date and property description to decimal, title certification, suspense rights, taxpayer ID, valuation and a notice of other statutory rights. Refuse an order padded beyond that list and the payer may not withhold solely for the refusal; refuse a clean seven-item order and it may hold your money without interest until you sign [DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:01:56]. Steven Hatcher, who has run an operator land department, adds that Louisiana makes it illegal to withhold funds over an unsigned division order, yet still lands on the practical play: if everything checks out, sign and send it in, because that is the easiest way to start receiving checks [Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:08:12]. Winblad goes the other way for Oklahoma, pointing to Hull v. Sun Refining, where withholding royalties over an unreturned division order was held to violate public policy and the company was ordered to pay the owner's attorney fees and costs, plus Oklahoma's 12 percent interest compounded annually on late payments [iD4uCjptCXM @ 00:03:22].

Practitioners also disagree on how hard a signature binds you. Royalty Clerk reads the Texas statute flat: a division order does not amend any lease, and either side can end it on 30 days written notice [DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:02:14]. The Energy Law Professor shows the case law is messier than the statute. In Gavenda v. Strata Energy, owners holding a full one-half nonparticipating royalty signed for 1/16 and took those checks for a couple of years, yet the Texas Supreme Court let them recover because the error was Strata's [YeBHUAmigMw @ 00:05:38]. But in Middleton, a market-value gas lease was effectively switched to contract-price payment by the signed division order, and the court let the division order control; the professor calls the two cases theoretically inconsistent, drawing the line at small, non-systematic differences versus big substantive ones [jZoApbdkCu0 @ 00:10:38]. Justin Williams, Matt Sands's co-host, warns that once signed, a division order stands for whatever percentage it says until revoked, and the oil company has no obligation to review it [inopKiaG-3A @ 00:23:30]. The working split: the statute treats the paper as harmless, while the case law and owner experience say a signed decimal and gas valuation method can stick until you act.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The number one mistake on Justin Williams's list is signing without verifying the decimal, followed by entity errors: a living trust and a trust after death can carry the same name and still cause a mess at tax time [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:31:17]. The overpayment trap is where signing blind gets expensive. Blue Mesa Minerals reports that when an operator later finds it overpaid, owners can go months or years with no royalty revenue while the account balances, and warns against any clause that puts the operator's errors on you, including its legal fees [SfX6ycoYg24 @ 00:02:51]. Steven Hatcher says the real commitment in most states is not to the acreage but to repaying or indemnifying the operator for overpayment, handled through suspense until recouped, and adds that operators have actually filed suit against lessors to recover funds [Z_HlEDh8-rw @ 00:07:42]. Matt Sands spells out the temptation: a division order shows a bigger number than you think you own and you just cash the checks, until the operator discovers you own 0.05 percent instead of 0.1 and withholds the difference until you make it whole [inopKiaG-3A @ 00:15:56]. The economics check is simple: a bigger decimal is not a windfall, it is a deferred clawback.

The second trap rides in the fine print. Blue Mesa Minerals refuses to sign division orders carrying cost-deduction language: if your lease is cost-free and the division order lets the operator deduct compression and cleaning costs, you have handed back what you negotiated, and Blue Mesa reports some operators taking 20 to 30 percent of royalties in deductions while others take up to 70 or 80 percent [SfX6ycoYg24 @ 00:05:26]. Royalty Clerk flags the same extra in Texas, a clause letting the payer take gathering, compression and processing costs whether or not your lease allows it, and notes such a term is invalid to the extent it contradicts the lease [DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:01:17]. Mineral View puts numbers on lease-driven bleed: $1.50 per barrel on 5,000 barrels a month strips $7,500 from the revenue base, and a 3 percent marketing fee on a $100,000 well removes $3,000 a month, or $36,000 a year, before royalty math starts [KYu7M4t5LAk @ 00:06:54]. The tax-side leak is just as mechanical: skip the W-9 and NARO says the payer must withhold 28 percent of royalty income for the IRS, so send it no matter what [W3POOsq6ka0 @ 00:01:31]. Each of these leaks repeats on every monthly check, so the deduction language gets read line by line against the lease before anything is signed.

The third cluster is plain clerical failure. Blue Mesa Minerals has seen decimals typed with one zero too many or too few, and errors that ran miscalculated for a long time until the owner did independent math [SfX6ycoYg24 @ 00:02:11]. Royalty Clerk lists the mistake versions of a changing decimal, a dropped digit or an old unit size, and shows why the fourth digit matters: on 10,000 barrels at $70, a decimal 2.7 percent low costs $18.59 a month on oil alone, while a lease promising 1/4 paid at the 1/8 number pays exactly half [blbomhUd0sA @ 00:02:45]. Matt Sands says that when a well changes hands the decimal should not change, and a mismatch is often the new operator loading its pay deck into accounting wrong, so compare old check stubs against the new division order [tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:36:08]. The clock is the final trap. Sands warns that waiting too long runs into statute of limitations and lost revenue, and Royalty Clerk's Texas timetable gives the yardstick: first payment within 120 days after the month of first sale, then oil within 60 days and gas within 90, with late payments owed interest at two percentage points above the New York Fed lending rate [SAMqfyu0Ovo @ 00:05:02].

callout.title: Four Hard Checks Before the Division Order Goes Back in the Mail
callout.body: Practitioners who have been burned by clawbacks, deduction clauses, withholding and pay deck errors run these four checks before any signature leaves the house.
items: Do not sign until your rebuilt decimal matches; if it does not, call the division order department and tell them they made a mistake or convince you that you are wrong [NARO — W3POOsq6ka0 @ 00:02:47].
Kill any clause that makes you liable for the operator's errors or its legal fees, and any cost-deduction language that contradicts a cost-free lease [Blue Mesa Minerals — SfX6ycoYg24 @ 00:03:12].
Return the W-9 no matter what, even on Oklahoma wells where you refuse to sign, or the company withholds the maximum amount the tax code requires [Richard Winblad — iD4uCjptCXM @ 00:09:16].
Treat a decimal that changes on a new operator's division order as a red flag and make the new operator show how it came up with the number [Matt Sands — tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:35:55].

action_checklist: Rebuild the decimal before signing: royalty fraction times net mineral acres divided by unit acres, so 1/4 times 5 over 1,280 is 0.0097656 [Royalty Clerk — DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:02:56].
Pull the unit size from the state oil and gas commission plat, permit, or the spacing and pooling order for the well [Matt Sands — tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:14:16].

Strike every non-statutory extra, initial each strike with a line saying you do not agree, and return it by a method with proof of delivery while keeping a copy [Royalty Clerk — DN-VIoSmyF0 @ 00:03:58].
If your numbers disagree, ask the operator for its documentation or a redacted copy of the title opinion pages covering your interest [Matt Sands — tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:24:40].
Compare the division order with the check stub, then compare check stub to check stub periodically to confirm the decimal has not moved [Matt Sands — tJr4jiz31fw @ 00:38:05].
If the decimal was wrong, demand corrected payments back to the first month it was wrong [Royalty Clerk — blbomhUd0sA @ 00:03:48].

chapters.question_prompt: What does a landman actually do, how do you become one, and how is mineral title run and cured?
chapters.title: Landmen and Title: From Courthouse to Curative
chapters.subtitle: A day in the life of a real landman, career levels and expectations vs. TV reality, AAPL career path, courthouse and digital landman tools, basic title and deed-chain exercises, Louisiana ownership, ethics in negotiation, title defects, curative measures and title shortcuts
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners converge on one job: run title from the patent or sovereignty forward, lease every owner in the unit, and cure defects so royalties get paid, because without confirmed rights an operator is trespassing. Trainers demand precision: never guess, work in fractions, watch for "of my interest," and expect Oklahoma payouts to the sixth decimal. The numbers: Courthouse Direct searches at $20 plus $0.10 per record, File Viewer at $100 for 300 views, title runs of 1-2 weeks clean and 3-5 weeks complex, and simple probates of $3,000-4,000 that can swamp a 0.1 net-acre interest. Practitioners split on how much a landman owes the other side, Jessup limiting it to truthful answers without interpretive analysis while McGuire calls for all the sound advice, and on whether contract land work or mineral buying is the better lane.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across the field, practitioners frame the landman as the person who makes a well legally drillable and payable. Steven Hatcher, who started at a law firm writing title opinions for large upstream operators, says landmen do "pretty much everything before drilling of any oil and gas well": figure out who owns the land, lease the owners, and then cure title defects after drilling "to make sure that everybody's getting paid" [ifwy0MQE0b4 @ 00:00:21]. Without confirmed rights, drilling through a tract is trespass, and the operator still has to know whom to pay royalties. Susan Jessup compresses the commercial point into a field slogan: "get that lease that's our bread and butter no lease no grease" [sldaaowniGM @ 00:12:19]. Hatcher's career videos make the same point, calling landmen "the dealmakers in oil and gas" because an oil company without rights to the land cannot drill [e1rml2NIbco @ 00:00:22]. The Untold Shifts narration opens with "Every oil deal begins here in the deed records" and closes, after recounting the record May 2026 BLM lease sale, on "Somebody reading old deeds very carefully" [mhaDQdLWgw0 @ 00:00:58]. The work starts in the courthouse, now often online, and covers every tract in the drilling unit before the first dollar moves.

The second point of agreement is that title work punishes guessing. The Landman Class instructor states flatly "we don't guess ever," citing "four hundred thousand dollar mistakes half a million dollar mistakes," and warns that a single guess can lose the client and the whole firm's jobs [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:35:50]. The same session stresses how fine the math gets: a 2.5-acre tract can carry 30 owners, and the "state of Oklahoma wants us to pay out to the sixth decimal place," which is why the instructor tells trainees to work in fractions because decimals occasionally fail [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:32:13]. The instructor also has crews shade maps to catch missed tracts before plats go out to clients. Sebastian Cosme drills the same discipline at the instrument level: "you can only deed out what you have," so the words "of my interest" in a deed change whether a grantor keeps 1/12 or nothing at all [-fWjBQtg9r4 @ 00:01:35]. Hatcher's law-firm years show the backstop: operators shipped "bankers boxes full of documents" to title attorneys whose job was "to make sure that the landmen did their jobs correctly" before drilling and division order opinions issued [ifwy0MQE0b4 @ 00:01:22]. Cosme's closing line could sit over every desk in the business: "this industry everything's important."

The third consensus point is that cashing royalty checks is not the same as owning clean title, and the operator's division order desk is the pressure point either way. Matt Sands and Justin Williams draw the line hard: operators pay at a "materially lower bar" driven by liability, while marketable title means no gaps, liens, or competing claims, and "You could be collecting checks for years while still not holding the marketable title for that property" [sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:22:57]. Buyers, they add, "apply the higher bar, not the operator's bar, and they pay a premium for marketable title." Clint Gust, the Denver attorney-landman on an earlier Sands episode, gives the first move for anyone holding inherited, producing minerals: review the vesting instrument, then contact the operator's division order analysts [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:29:35]. Chris McGuire, 18 years in the field including in-house stints at ConocoPhillips and Energy Transfer, tells owners to notify the operator about any sale or death, noting operators have "whole floors of people that do nothing but try to keep that intact" [gsOnEm_adKI @ 00:34:50]. Suspended money is treated as escrow rather than a penalty, Sands says ("They're not taking money from you"), but Gust warns unclaimed payments can go to the state after a period such as five years [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:32:37].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Reading land starts with the survey grid. The Landman Class instructor teaches Oklahoma off an initial point about 6 miles west of Davis, with townships of 6 by 6 miles holding 36 sections of about 640 acres each, numbered from the northeast corner [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:05:47]. To locate T14N R13E, count 14 times 6 miles north and 13 times 6 miles east, and always convert to feet at 5,280 per mile because "they want feet always." In a legal description, two directional modifiers mean a quarter and one means a half [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:13:48]. The northern and western correction rows (sections 1-6, 18, 19, 30, 31) hold lots of roughly 40 acres plus or minus, Section 6 is a double correction, and lot acreage should always be checked against the 1870s BLM survey. Plot descriptions right-to-left, largest unit first, and treat a semicolon as the break between tracts [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:38:40]; deliverables go out as Excel plats. On conveyances, Cosme's worked example is the one to memorize: if John Smith owns 1/6 of the NW quarter and deeds "an undivided one half interest" to Kevin Baker, Smith is left with nothing and Baker takes the full 1/6, but "one half of my interest" leaves each with 1/12 [-fWjBQtg9r4 @ 00:00:46].

For records, Paul Cones of Courthouse Direct in Houston walks through a paid stack with hard prices. A Reeves County legal-description search returned 439 results for $63.90, built as a $20 base plus $0.10 per record, and Cones admits that a zero-result screen "typically means you probably entered the information in the wrong box and that's what I did" [822U1_i8V5Q @ 00:20:42]. Party-name searches are free, indexes are free to view, and charges run per image view rather than per page. File Viewer runs $100 a month for 300 views and $0.50 per view after that, or a $50 daily pass covering 100 records or 24 hours, whichever comes first; heavy users pulling more than 200 documents a month can take Texas Volume Plus at $0.50 per document against a $200 monthly minimum [822U1_i8V5Q @ 00:55:28]. Title plants cost $500 a month plus $50 per user, with Reeves County at $1,000 a month. The free Lease Alert sends 2-3 emails a week, and a spike of 500 leases marks where the action is [822U1_i8V5Q @ 00:43:31]. Beyond Texas, Clint Gust points to the paid Weld County online recorder, okcountyrecords.com for a fee, and a plain Google search of "county, state, property records" [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:37:41].

Curative runs on a clock and a price list. Clint Gust quotes about 1-2 weeks for clean title and 3-5 weeks for nasty chains reaching back to the early 1900s, with a working ballpark of "two weeks to four weeks" [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:11:42]. Ambiguous instruments get a corrective instrument, or alternatively a stipulation of interest and cross-conveyance [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:16:22]. Affidavits of heirship will not pass marketable title on their own in Colorado or Wyoming, yet in hot areas operators lease the heirs anyway, carry the risk, and demand probate or a heirship determination before paying. Matt Sands prices the alternative: a simple probate runs about $3,000-4,000, which can exceed the value of a 0.1 net-acre interest [sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:14:16]. State rules swing the math. A Texas affidavit becomes definitive evidence 5 years after recording, not after death; Oklahoma wants 10 years on file and no will for marketable title; Colorado wants 20 years on record; and Texas-only muniment of title requires no unpaid debts and a filing within 4 years of death. The shortcut both Sands and Williams endorse is the "cheat code": ask the operator or division order analyst exactly what document and language they will accept before drafting anything [sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:16:13].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the courthouse-to-curative chain is how much a landman owes the person across the table. Susan Jessup draws a hard line: honesty does not mean handing over confidential information, and a landman has no duty to give the other side interpretive analysis of the lease [sldaaowniGM @ 00:10:43]. Her working rule is practical disclosure: do not volunteer everything, but when asked a specific question, answer truthfully with nothing added [sldaaowniGM @ 00:37:30]. Chris McGuire, an 18-year landman who worked in-house at ConocoPhillips and Energy Transfer, frames the job differently on the RE: Real Estate Podcast, saying the landman owes all the sound advice and that the job is to make sure the deal is a win-win for everybody [gsOnEm_adKI @ 00:36:21]. The Untold Shifts narration leans toward McGuire at the family table: families are the hardest part, and the narrated landman tells the owner to have a lawyer read the lease [mhaDQdLWgw0 @ 00:04:59]. A Jessup-style shop scripts anonymous-client calls, avoids coercive phrases, and keeps interpretation off the table; a McGuire-style shop builds trust by explaining bonus, royalty and override math in plain terms. Both camps agree the lease is the product; they differ on how much analysis rides along with it.

On how to break in and which lane to run, the practitioners pull in opposite directions. AAPL's own profile tells newcomers the first step is to join AAPL and then pursue certification, pitching a typical landman wage of $126,000 and fast promotion as 1980s-boom landmen retire [AJGoTBiN9oQ @ 00:08:18]. The Landman Class instructor flatly rejects paper as a door-opener: a certificate will not get you a job; you email, phone the next day, and show up, the way Sebastian did in 2007 with 20 minutes to spare [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:01:16]. Steven Hatcher splits the field into independent lease brokers, in-house landmen, and mineral buyers, calls in-house seats more coveted and harder to get, and argues the buyer-broker lane is best because it lets a buyer buy, partner, or flip and generate their own opportunities [1hz9VkFL01Y @ 00:01:50]. Some of the best landmen Hatcher knows never went to college, and what matters is how fast you learn and whether you can find deals [kA4imCIrIU0 @ 00:02:19]. The practical read: AAPL sells the credential ladder and the compensation survey; Landman Class and Hatcher sell hustle and deal flow, and the Hatcher lane only pays once the hardest step, finding the deal, gets solved.

The deepest technical split is how much paper an heir needs before money moves. Clint Gust, an attorney-landman with Northstar Energy in Denver, says an affidavit of death and heirship passes marketable title in some states but on its own will not in Colorado or Wyoming [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:12:51]. Yet in hot areas, Gust reports, operators lease the heirs anyway, eat the risk, and only demand probate or a heirship determination before paying. Matt Sands and Justin Williams map a wider patchwork: Texas treats a recorded affidavit as definitive evidence after five years on record, Oklahoma uses it to release suspense or support a lease, North Dakota accepts it for small multigeneration estates, New Mexico uses an affidavit of succession, and Colorado wants 20 years on record [sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:13:33]. Their cheat code cuts through the patchwork: ask the operator or the division order analyst exactly which document and language they will accept [sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:16:13]. On do-it-yourself work, Gust warns of spinning wheels and tells owners to build a baseline, then hire a landman before any net-mineral-acre deal [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:18:59], while Sands features a listener named David filing his own Colorado probates from sample forms.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures start at the desk, not the rig. The Landman Class instructor says the firm never guesses because they have seen four hundred thousand dollar and half-a-million dollar mistakes, and one guess can lose the client and every job the firm holds with them [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:35:50]. The same instructor warns that decimals occasionally fail, so landmen must teach themselves fractions, which matters when a 2.5-acre tract can carry 30 owners and Oklahoma pays to the sixth decimal place [ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:34:47]. Sebastian Cosme shows the trap in one deed: if John Smith owns 1/6 of the northwest quarter and deeds an undivided one-half interest to Kevin Baker, Smith is left with nothing and Baker takes the full 1/6, because you can only deed out what you have; deed one half of my interest instead and each holds 1/12 [-fWjBQtg9r4 @ 00:01:35]. Hatcher, who began writing drilling and division order title opinions at a law firm, spells out the downstream cost: without confirmed rights, drilling through a tract is trespass, and the operator still has to know exactly whom to pay [ifwy0MQE0b4 @ 00:01:36]. Miss the words of my interest and every royalty decimal below that deed is wrong.

The second trap is mistaking a check for a title. Matt Sands puts it bluntly: you could be collecting checks for years while still not holding marketable title, because operators pay at a materially lower bar built around whether anybody will credibly sue them, while buyers apply the higher bar and pay a premium for marketable title [sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:22:57]. A paid-but-defensible interest draws discounted offers, and one heir's gaps can stall a whole family's sale. The math can also turn against curative: a simple probate runs about $3,000 to $4,000, which can exceed the value of a 0.1 net-acre interest, and an affidavit accepted on a $25-a-year vertical well can be re-reviewed the moment horizontal wells worth $10,000 or more show up [sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:28:04]. Clint Gust adds the clock: under unclaimed property laws, suspended payments can go to the state after a period such as five years [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:32:37]. When an operator simply refuses to pay, Gust says a letter from an attorney carrying a potential threat of litigation can be enough to push the operator over the edge [zoP-dgL5D7M @ 00:36:12]. Suspense itself works like escrow, not a penalty.

On the buying side, the failures are about time and liquidity. Kevin Jones, the mayor Hatcher bought out in Harrison County, Ohio, describes leasing for a share of the wellhead only to watch checks fall to about $1,000 every couple of months once the market dropped and operators curved the wells [lCpJ3rpcfvY @ 00:45:30]. Jones also sold a 12% royalty interest early on; the land was later drilled through 21 acres and, by Jones's account, could have paid about $15,000 a month, and a Chesapeake lease once defaulted on a $27,000 bonus before the minerals reverted to Jones. Hatcher's own guardrail is that minerals that never get developed have zero value, and there is no Zillow for minerals to tell a good deal from one where you lose your shirt [p0bOEBxdOFs @ 00:02:38]. In Hatcher's valuation model, volume, price and time drive the number, and time, meaning when the wells get drilled, matters most [H6l9yCZoYDQ @ 00:06:05]. Data costs bite too: Courthouse Direct's no-minimum per-page plan gets expensive on a 100-page assignment, and a search that returns zero results usually means the information went in the wrong box [822U1_i8V5Q @ 00:54:07].

callout.title: Stop-checks before a run sheet, lease or check goes out the door
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, reversal or near-miss the practitioners lived through. Clear all four before committing money, signatures or a division order decimal.
items: No fraction leaves the desk as a guess; work every interest in fractions and verify it, because the firm has watched four hundred thousand and half-million dollar mistakes cost clients [Landman Class — ibeQr-rDmZ4 @ 00:35:50].

Confirm mineral owner permission on every tract in the drilling unit before the bit turns, because drilling through unleased tracts is trespass and the operator must know whom to pay [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — ifwy0MQE0b4 @ 00:01:36].
Price curative against the interest before filing anything: a simple probate at about $3,000 to $4,000 can exceed the value of a 0.1 net-acre interest [Matt Sands — sB8BNPnN_Os @ 00:14:16].
Never edit a signed instrument to fix a missing capacity; go back and re-obtain the signature, as Jessup did on a missing trustee capacity [Susan Jessup — sldaaowniGM @ 00:32:23].

chapters.question_prompt: How are the wells under my minerals drilled and completed, and what do the major shale plays look like?
chapters.title: How Wells Get Drilled: Horizontal Technology and the Major Shale Plays
chapters.subtitle: Vertical, deviated, directional and horizontal wells, the annulus, horizontal drilling and frac stimulation, options for depleted wells, high build-rate Marcellus wells, gas EOR in the Permian, and the Utica, Marcellus and Permian Basin plays
chapters.executive_summary: Operators across Expand Energy, Chesapeake, Range Resources and the British Columbia Energy Regulator describe the same drilling sequence: conductor, surface casing set below the deepest fresh water, a vertical section stopped a few hundred feet above the shale, a gradual build curve steered by an adjustable-bend motor or rotary steerable system, then a cemented production string and plug-and-perf stimulation. The numbers are specific: 21 to 28 rig days, laterals up to 28,000 ft, one pad replacing 32 vertical wells on 1,280 acres with 90% less surface disturbance. Play-level data shows Utica laterals doubling since 2017 and Marcellus pads costing up to $70 million. Disagreements surface over conductor depths, lateral lengths, mud versus air intervals, and whether geology or technology deserves credit for the shale boom.

key_metrics.label: Continuous Rig Time Per Well
key_metrics.value: 24 hours a day, 7 days a week for approximately 21 to 28 days
key_metrics.context: Expand Energy's stated rig duration for drilling a typical horizontal natural gas well from spud to total depth.

key_metrics.label: Pad Consolidation on a 1,280-Acre Tract
key_metrics.value: Up to 32 vertical wells on separate pads replaced by one multi-well horizontal pad, 90% less surface disturbance
key_metrics.context: Chesapeake field comparison of vertical versus horizontal development recovering the same natural gas reserves.

key_metrics.label: Utica Lateral Length Benchmark
key_metrics.value: Nearly 9 out of 10 wells drilled in 2025 had laterals longer than 12,500 ft
key_metrics.context: Mark Roach's account of Utica laterals roughly doubling since 2017 and growing about 40% since 2020.

key_metrics.value: Upwards of $60 million, maybe even $70 million

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator walk-through starts with the same steel telescope. Expand Energy drills a large-diameter hole for the first 90 to 110 ft before the rig even arrives, cements conductor casing, then air or freshwater drills until the bit clears the base of the freshwater zone, after which surface casing is cemented inside the conductor [zhTs0NrEVgE @ 00:01:15]. The Chesapeake version of the same sequence puts the Marcellus freshwater zone at roughly 800 ft and air drills an average of 100 to 200 ft below its base before setting surface casing [7tXxUXv528A @ 00:01:12]. Range Resources showed the physical hardware on a Marcellus pad: a 26-inch line for the first 40 ft, a 20-inch water string set to 401 ft at that location based on the nearby water table, a 13 3/8 mine string to isolate coal, a 9 5/8 intermediate, and 5 1/2 inch production casing to total depth [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:05:23]. The British Columbia Energy Regulator describes the same logic from the regulator's chair: surface casing isolates fresh water and serves as the foundation for the blowout preventer, with cement pumped out the shoe and forced up between casing and hole [qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:00:47]. Nobody skips a layer; the debate is only depth.

The second point of agreement is where and how the well turns. Expand stops the assembly a few hundred feet above the target shale, trips the string out, and swaps to either a rotary steerable system or a downhole motor with an adjustable bend to steer from vertical to horizontal [zhTs0NrEVgE @ 00:03:41]. The British Columbia Energy Regulator puts the kickoff point at approximately 500 feet above the planned horizontal leg, runs a downhole motor with measurement-while-drilling instruments, and says the curve from kickoff to horizontal takes just under a quarter of a mile [qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:01:26]. Range Resources hammers the same misconception every visitor brings: it is not an abrupt 90 degree bend but a slow, gradual build over several hundred feet, and the one-degree bend at the bottom of the motor lets the crew turn that bend any direction they want to steer [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:17:08]. Range also claims its crews could hit a basketball buried 2 miles deep and 2 miles out, using pulses sent through the drilling mud, the earth's magnetic pull, and formation calculations, all checked by human monitors [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:16:15]. The operating rule is simple: get vertical to the kickoff point cheap, then build the curve slow and controlled.

The business case is identical across every speaker: contact. Chesapeake's field script says horizontal wells touch more gas-producing shale, so fewer wells develop a field, and one multi-well pad can recover the same reserves from a 1,280-acre tract that would otherwise need as many as 32 vertical wells on their own pads, cutting surface disturbance by 90% [7tXxUXv528A @ 00:05:10]. Energy Vision Global frames it as the vertical well crossing the formation over a short interval while the horizontal stays inside the reservoir for a much longer distance, which is why it pays in thin reservoirs and developments where production efficiency is critical, at the cost of advanced directional tools and accurate real-time measurements [fihgFZ8xpQo @ 00:05:49]. Petro Learn adds that shale and tight oil sit in narrow layers, so the lateral exposes far more wellbore to oil-rich rock and significantly increases production rates [Xr_kSHJguTM @ 00:02:57]. The British Columbia Energy Regulator closes the loop: tight reservoirs lack natural fractures and cannot be produced economically without hydraulic fracturing, and multi-stage fracking is now the standard [qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:04:57]. Horizontal reach without stimulation is just an expensive hole drilled through rock that will not flow.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Range Resources splits the job across two rigs to save money. A conventional air rig, a Falcon Drilling unit built by Shram, drills the vertical sections and sets most of the casing strings on every well on the pad because it is more cost efficient than the larger horizontal rig; crews work 12-hour shifts and the rig moves on after a couple of weeks [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:11:39]. The horizontal rig then arrives; Range favors a super single only 90 ft tall that it calls nimbler, a lot cheaper, and more welcome to neighbors [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:18:18]. Bit selection follows the hole section: roller cone tricone and hammer bits in the vertical air-drilled portion, then synthetic-diamond PDC bits that shave the shale in the lateral, with mud jetted through the nozzles to cool the bit and carry cuttings [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:09:40]. The British Columbia Energy Regulator supplies the tubular math: 30-foot joints at roughly 495 pounds each, over 350 joints weighing nearly 87 tons for a 10,500-foot well, with the string pulled for bit and tool changes in a process called tripping pipe [qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:02:07]. Every trip is rig time, so the bit plan matters.

The mechanics that keep the lateral alive live in the annulus. Offshore Engineering Academy gives the driller's formula: hole diameter squared minus pipe diameter squared, divided by 1029.4, equals annular volume in barrels per foot, so a 12 1/4 inch hole around 5 inch pipe runs about 0.12 barrels per foot [YPFuHij-FYk @ 00:03:00]. That number is the first line of defense against a blowout: if returns do not match what was pumped, the crew is either losing fluid into the rock or taking a kick, and both are stop-everything emergencies [YPFuHij-FYk @ 00:03:48]. The same channel warns that bigger pipe in the same hole speeds annular velocity and cleans the hole, but extra friction pressure can fracture weak rock, so hole cleaning versus breaking the hole is a constant balancing act. Dennis Livingston, the Baker Hughes automated drilling systems technical advisor, describes the team with Consol Energy hitting two-mile-a-day Marcellus wells drilled under Pittsburgh International Airport, where the hard part was building a high dogleg curve into a long lateral at proper ROP, landing in target and staying there [40uE_5Fvn_A @ 00:01:09]. The stated lesson from that record run was three words repeated: plan, plan, plan, with operator, service company, office and rig personnel aligned on goals and communication holding through execution [40uE_5Fvn_A @ 00:01:45].

Once production casing is cemented, the rig leaves and the service crew takes over. The British Columbia Energy Regulator lays out the cycle: a perforating gun goes down on wireline, an electrical charge shoots holes through casing and cement into the shale, the stage is fracked with water, sand and additives at extremely high pressure, a temporary plug isolates it, and the sequence repeats until the lateral is covered, after which the plugs are drilled out [qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:03:41]. Range Resources showed the hardware: perf guns with angled charges blasting a few inches to a few feet into the Marcellus, a frac plug set in place, a frac ball dropped to control the next stage, and a small drilling unit grinding everything into material that looks like sawdust [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:31:51]. Range's fluid is 99.9% water and sand with three to four chemicals: an antimicrobial, a scale inhibitor and a friction reducer [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:30:13]. Water travels five to seven miles from centralized impoundments through temporary pipeline, 25 to 30% of it recycled, and fracking one well while prepping the next raised some efficiencies by a factor of four [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:21:40]. Each stage is controlled from the frac van, where crews can shut the whole spread down remotely.

callout.title: Cost and surveillance moves operators actually use
callout.body: Four field-tested edges pulled from rig floors, frac sites, pilot surveillance and core libraries.
items: Run a cheaper air rig for every vertical section on the pad and save the big horizontal rig for the laterals; Range calls the vertical rigs more cost efficient than the larger rigs that drill the horizontals [Range Resources Corporation — 8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:11:39]

Reverse an existing pipeline to power the rig on field gas: scrub liquids out in wet gas areas, run it through a conversion kit in place of diesel, and cut fuel cost because the gas is cheaper [Range Resources Corporation — 8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:19:26]

Watch intermediate casing pressure even on strings that receive no gas directly; Chevron saw it rise during injection from heat and conduction and flagged unmonitored pressure as a path to casing failure [Whitson Academy — r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:18:12]

Pull legacy cuttings before committing to a zone: Premier analyzed four Wolfcamp wells in Eddy and Lee County and found two great, one marginal and one poor even though open hole logs looked fairly similar [Hart Energy — KynEhshipEg @ 00:07:18]

sop_steps.title: Front-end science, permits and pad capital
sop_steps.action: Study the rock, topography and regulatory requirements before any surface work begins.
sop_steps.detail: Range magnifies the shale tens of thousands of times to read organic content, files water sourcing, recycling and construction plans, and handles sound studies, traffic reports and road bonding, with planning beginning up to three years ahead on a pad worth upwards of $60 to $70 million [Range Resources Corporation — 8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:04:34]

sop_steps.title: Shallow hole and freshwater isolation
sop_steps.action: Set conductor, air drill below the freshwater base, then cement surface casing and install the BOP.
sop_steps.detail: Chesapeake air drills an average of 100 to 200 ft below the base of a Marcellus freshwater zone that runs to approximately 800 ft, then cements surface casing inside the conductor before the blowout preventer goes on [Oil & Gas Industry VDA — 7tXxUXv528A @ 00:01:31]

sop_steps.title: Kickoff, build curve and lateral
sop_steps.action: Stop above the target, trip out, run a steerable assembly and build angle into the shale.
sop_steps.detail: Drill to the kickoff point about 500 feet above the planned leg, run a downhole motor with measurement while drilling instruments, build the curve over just under a quarter mile, then drill the lateral to target distance [British Columbia Energy Regulator — qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:01:48]

sop_steps.title: Case, perf, frac and drill out
sop_steps.action: Cement production casing full length, then perforate and frac stage by stage behind plugs.
sop_steps.detail: Perf and frac each stage, isolate it with a temporary plug, repeat across the entire horizontal distance, and drill out the plugs so gas can flow up the wellbore [British Columbia Energy Regulator — qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:05:17]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Operators split on the hardware that turns the hole from vertical to lateral. Expand Energy stops the assembly a few hundred feet above the target shale, trips the string, and swaps to either a rotary steerable system or a downhole motor with an adjustable bend, then drills laterals up to 28,000 ft from the point of formation entry [zhTs0NrEVgE @ 00:03:57]. Range Resources runs the motor route: a one-degree bend at the bottom of the assembly that crews rotate to steer, building a slow, gradual curve over several hundred feet instead of an abrupt 90-degree turn [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:17:08]. Baker Hughes and Consol Energy took the other path beneath Pittsburgh International Airport, deploying high build-rate rotary steerable systems to land a high dogleg curve, stay in the target zone, and post two-mile-a-day wells in the Marcellus [40uE_5Fvn_A @ 00:01:45]. Even there, Denise Livingston names teamwork as the main key factor, with aligned goals between office staff, rig crews, operator, and service company, and reduces the lesson to one instruction: plan, plan, plan. The British Columbia Energy Regulator sequence sets the kickoff point roughly 500 ft above the planned horizontal leg and budgets just under a quarter mile from kickoff to horizontal using a downhole motor carrying measurement-while-drilling instruments [qSA8EoDzhKo @ 00:01:26].

Lateral length is the loudest split between the legacy playbook and the current one. Chesapeake's Marcellus method drills horizontally for more than 4,000 ft past formation entry, then cements production casing to roughly 2,500 ft above the producing shale or all the way to surface depending on regional geology [7tXxUXv528A @ 00:04:00]. Range Resources prices the payoff of that older geometry: its 4,000-ft laterals, each wellbore running down a mile and out about half a mile, total around 11 to 12 billion cubic feet equivalent, enough for one pad to fuel more than a quarter million homes over the next decade [8M30VzyjEpk @ 00:45:02]. Mark Roach of FutureWise Energy reports the Utica pushing far past that: average laterals roughly doubled since 2017, nearly nine of ten 2025 wells exceeded 12,500 ft, and Ascent Resources averaged just over 16,000 ft, putting more rock behind every set of fixed costs, though Roach notes they also demand serious planning for surface rights and infrastructure [nbj7-lPJ59w @ 00:11:46]. Expand Energy frames the same lever at the land level: a 1,280-acre tract that might need 32 vertical wells on 32 pads can be drained from one multi-well horizontal pad with 90 percent less surface disturbance [zhTs0NrEVgE @ 00:05:09].

Chevron's Permian team broke from the CO2 playbook on enhanced recovery. Lab studies and a Midland Basin field pilot proved CO2 huff-and-puff in horizontal shale wells improved long-term recovery, but high CO2 retention in the reservoir, the cost of the commodity, and pipelines missing from much of the basin pushed the team to compress and reinject its own produced hydrocarbon gas instead [r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:07:11]. Dvesh Kumar's group also rejects soak time, finding that adding a day or a week never changed the response materially, so Chevron treats soak time as optional rather than a value lever [r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:52:31]. Energy Window Insights draws a harder line inside the depleted-reservoir menu: single-phase MPD holds bottom-hole pressure nearly constant with surface back pressure, but back pressure only adds pressure and cannot remove it, and MPD is not a well control method; underbalanced drilling flows the reservoir on purpose to cut damage, losses, and differential sticking, but forfeits its benefits the moment underbalance is lost [aY0LJMEZzZo @ 00:01:18]. On target screening, the Premier sample library team in Midland found four New Mexico wells that looked fairly similar on open-hole logs, yet archived cuttings sorted them into two great, one marginal, and one poor [KynEhshipEg @ 00:07:34].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Misreading the rock is the oldest and costliest trap in these plays. Range Resources' Renns No. 1 well in Mount Pleasant Township, Washington County was drilled as a structural test of the Westland Dome to 8,470 ft; millions spent, nothing commercial, site restored, the well slated to be plugged and abandoned as a write-off [oSSTf7vpnpU @ 00:02:51]. Geologist Bill Zagorski argued for one more attempt, and the October 2004 frac of the Marcellus and Skaneateles interval made about 300,000 cubic feet a day from a vertical hole with a small treatment. GeoScope adds the flip side: clay-rich shale deforms, absorbs the pumped energy, and closes when pressure drops, so an operator can spend a fortune and get nothing back [oSSTf7vpnpU @ 00:11:14]. GeoFins reports that Wolfberry wells drilled since the 1980s passed straight through the Wolfcamp, treating it as one ingredient in a stacked vertical completion rather than a target in its own right [xL3_8adbQ4Q @ 00:02:01]. The data trap compounds it. A Permian geologist on Hart Energy's Premier segment warns that collecting samples while drilling is the one time you can get actual rock data from a well you drill, and skipping sample capture means never having it [KynEhshipEg @ 00:05:06].

Inside the wellbore, the failures are quieter. Chevron's five-year Permian pilot found intermediate casing pressure climbing during injection even though that string takes no gas directly, driven by heat and conduction, and warns that unmonitored it can lead to casing failure [r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:18:31]. Compressor downtime was the other early bleed: every shutdown dropped reservoir pressure and burned project time rebuilding it, which is why runtime became a success metric [r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:19:46]. Without daily well tests in the first days of flowback, the oil spike that carries the uplift is easy to miss; Kumar calls high-frequency early testing incredibly important despite how basic it looks. Offshore Engineering Academy frames the drilling version: if returning mud does not match pumped volume, the hole is either losing expensive fluid to fractures or taking a kick of pressurized gas, both stop-everything emergencies, and annular volume math of hole diameter squared minus pipe diameter squared divided by 1029.4 is the first line of defense against a blowout [YPFuHij-FYk @ 00:03:48]. Swap to bigger pipe and annular velocity rises, cleaning the hole but raising friction pressure enough to fracture weak rock; widen the annulus and cuttings settle and pack off the well [YPFuHij-FYk @ 00:05:42].

The economics checks are blunt. Mark Roach traces Chesapeake from leasing well over a million net acres in eastern Ohio to a 2014-2016 crash in which oil fell from around $100 to the $20s and $30s, the US rig count dropped roughly 80 percent, and over-levered players came under real stress [nbj7-lPJ59w @ 00:06:28]. Chesapeake sold its Ohio Utica assets to Encino in 2018 for about $2 billion; EOG then paid $5.6 billion in 2025 to buy Encino itself, picking up roughly 675,000 net core acres. Roach flags the remaining ceilings: dry gas economics hinge on Henry Hub, ultra-long laterals require stitching surface rights across multiple parcels that slows permitting, and deep Utica wells at 10,000 to 12,000 ft are still high-cost appraisal [nbj7-lPJ59w @ 00:27:21]. Chevron's pilot shows depletion catching up with enhanced recovery: gas utility factor improved through year three as cycles increased, then ticked up in years four and five despite even more cycles, marking the point where the physics of a depleting reservoir takes over [r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:27:31]. And shutting in a well for flush production is not recovery at all; it only trades energy in time, while gas injection leaves a permanent wedge [r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:47:27].
