callout.title: Four Checks Before Capital Goes Downhole
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, near-miss, or blind spot practitioners hit in the field. Clear all four before committing rig days, frac spreads, or compressor horsepower.
items: Freeze the decline-curve baseline before the first injection cycle touches any connected well, then measure uplift at the tank level instead of the single well [Whitson Academy — r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:14:03].
Monitor intermediate casing pressure through every injection cycle, because heat and conduction can push it up and lead to casing failure [Whitson Academy — r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:18:50].
Reconcile mud returns against pumped volume on every circulation, because a mismatch means either losses or a kick [Offshore Engineering Academy — YPFuHij-FYk @ 00:03:48].

Screen candidate benches with physical cuttings, not open-hole logs alone, after four similar-looking logs split into two great, one marginal, and one poor well [Hart Energy — KynEhshipEg @ 00:07:34].

chapters.pull_quote: "You don't fight containment, you learn to live with it. So the easiest way is to get a bigger compressor." — Whitson Academy (r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:52:52).
action_checklist: Run annular volume math before each hole section: hole diameter squared minus pipe diameter squared, divided by 1029.4, gives barrels per foot, about 0.12 for a 12.25-inch hole with 5-inch pipe [Offshore Engineering Academy — YPFuHij-FYk @ 00:03:00].
Screen every trajectory from the target and its constraints first, then record one technical advantage and one tradeoff for the chosen shape [Carbon Strata Solutions — a-Ltd9yb7JI @ 00:01:28].

Plan jointly across operator, service company, office, and rig personnel, then carry the same communication into execution on high dogleg, long-lateral wells [Drilling Contractor Magazine — 40uE_5Fvn_A @ 00:02:03].
Mud log every well drilled and store the cuttings in a sample library for paleontology and geochemical analysis [Hart Energy — KynEhshipEg @ 00:05:22].
Run daily well tests in early flowback after each injection cycle, then space testing out to every three or four days or weekly [Whitson Academy — r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:17:08].
Set injection targets as cumulative volume placed over a 30-day window rather than peak daily rate, sized to the compressor and reservoir connectivity [Whitson Academy — r0aIro_ccSI @ 00:50:39].

chapters.question_prompt: Why do royalty checks decline, and how do decline curves, type curves and well performance drive mineral value?
chapters.title: Decline Curves, Well Performance and Mineral Valuation
chapters.subtitle: Life of a well, decline curve analysis in Danomics and Citrine, economic rate with oil and gas streams, type curves, shale performance drivers, Haynesville top wells, drilling costs, negative gas prices, royalty economics, and how activity drives mineral value
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree that modern shale wells front-load their value. Steven Hatcher says 70-80% of volume comes in the first two years, Mr. Business models a 60-70% first-year decline, and Troy Eckard warns that the first royalty check bundles one to five months of production. The street toolkit is Arps-style decline curve analysis: hyperbolic fits with b capped near 1.3, exponential tails around 8%, flowback excluded, and economic limits solved where revenue equals operating cost. TopDogEngineer used that method to reach 140.3 bbl/month. Valuation layers price and development timing on the curve, from Matt Sands's 50-70x three-month-royalty multiple up to full NPV10 builds. Disagreements center on three questions: whether to fit an average type curve or each well, whether type curves are useful for PDP, and how far auction comps can be trusted.

key_metrics.label: Shale two-year recovery share
key_metrics.value: 70-80% of total well volume within the first two years of production
key_metrics.context: Hatcher's rule of thumb for shale wells. He uses it to explain why mineral value peaks in the months right after first production.

key_metrics.label: Producing royalty valuation multiple
key_metrics.value: 50-70x the average of the last 3 months of royalty, up to 100x in hot areas
key_metrics.context: Sands's quick rule of thumb for valuing mature producing mineral assets before a full engineering valuation is run.

key_metrics.label: DIY decline fit constraints
key_metrics.value: b-factor below 1.3 with an 8% terminal decline
key_metrics.context: Sands's settings for a one-month Well Database DIY forecast exported to Excel. He calls 8% a good conservative number for most wells.

key_metrics.label: Economic limit rate
key_metrics.value: 140.3 bbl/month
key_metrics.context: Breakeven oil rate from a Solver run on q*Poil + q*GOR*Pgas - OpEx = 0, using a net gas price of about $2.067/Mcf. Below this rate the well loses money.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who talks about well performance describes the same shape: the money arrives early and the curve bends hard. Troy Eckard contrasts the shale era with vintage wells that started near 400 bbl/day and bled down to 25-50 bbl/day by roughly year 14. Modern high-IP wells let the operator target payback inside 36 months and then fund wells #2-5 on the same pad [nn1juJ3_-WA @ 00:05:58]. Steven Hatcher gives the rule of thumb that a shale well recovers 70 to 80 percent of its total volume within the first two years of production [CiR-w5lHfvI @ 00:11:46]. The Crude Files puts a number on a single Midland well: it peaks around 730 bbl/d and drops more than 70% inside year one. The channel's summary is 'the money is spent at the start, the oil comes fast, and then slows' [R-AasPj-Y5E @ 00:14:43]. Mr. Business pegs first-year decline at 60-70%, followed by several percent per year, and calls horizontal shale wells 'especially dramatic' [hIerB5MQ52U @ 00:11:25]. The consequence for the owner is the first-check trap. Eckard warns that the first check covers one to five months of production and lands about six months after start. The next check covers a single month, so it can look like a third or a sixth of the first.

The second point of agreement is that decline curve analysis is a forecasting method, not a guess. Matt Sands says the process works 'no matter what type of well' and applies to roughly 95% of wells. The exceptions are enhanced recovery such as waterflood or CO2, pipeline curtailment, and flat water-drive production [VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:06:59]. He traces the method from Arps in 1945 to Fetkovich in the 1980s. The working shape is a two-part fit: hyperbolic early, then an exponential tail at 8-15% per year, read on a semi-log scale. Francis Ramos II insists on a diagnostic check before any exponential math. Rate versus cumulative production should plot as a straight line, and rate versus time on a semi-log plot should be a straight line with a similar slope. A plain linear rate-time chart 'doesn't really tell you' whether the decline is exponential [u3kTgNXLIGI @ 00:02:28]. Once the decline is confirmed, he says you can estimate cumulative production 'without even drilling the well.' Mergers & Inquisitions defines the type curve as initial production plus its decline. In its model, that curve drives the revenue, expense, and capex estimates for each well, and the wells are then aggregated with OFFSET [2tJpxiIqFSM @ 00:01:00]. All three treat the decline curve as the foundation for every number that follows.

On valuation, the consensus is that a decline curve is worthless until price and timing are layered on top. Steven Hatcher compresses it to 'high prices plus High activity equals high value.' He argues that undeveloped minerals carry zero value until development is in sight, and that value peaks in the months after first production [CiR-w5lHfvI @ 00:00:48]. In his valuation episode, Matt Sands lays out the income, or engineering, approach: pick analog wells, adjust for one- or two-mile laterals, build a type curve, apply spacing and timing, and compute NPV [86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:15:30]. In a later episode he adds that value scales roughly linearly with price. Moving the price deck from $60 to $80 lifts value about 1.3x, and dropping from $80 to $60 leaves about 75% [VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:33:18]. Mr. Business warns that a $2,000 check from a six-month-old well overstates future income. That is why professionals run decline curve analysis and PV10 and apply a discount to undrilled locations [8gaFGCKNpnk @ 00:12:28]. Without the curve, the number on the check tells an owner little about future income. With the curve, a price deck, and a development timeline, it becomes a defensible valuation.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The fitting work is done in software, within set constraints. Matt Sands describes the two levers: initial decline sets the steepness, and the b-factor sets the bend, usually between 0 and 2. A b of 1 is harmonic decline, and a b of 0 is exponential [VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:19:57]. For a DIY run he points to Well Database on a one-month subscription. He caps b below 1.3 and sets an 8% terminal decline, then exports to Excel and multiplies by the owner's decimal interest. He calls 8% 'a good conservative number for most wells.' Danomics applies a similar constraint set in its Flows tool: Di left open, b bounded at 0-1.3, and a qi factor of 2x the maximum observed rate. On the 1.3 bound, the presenter adds, 'I'm not saying that is the correct value.' The tool declines roughly 4,000 wells in seconds and exports qi, Di, and b to CSV [gleafhkBQWg @ 00:03:45]. The choice of start method matters. Max is the default, First decline handles capacity-limited, choked gas wells, and Best fit suits late-time PDP packages. KAPPA Engineering's CITRINE excludes early flowback before fitting and weights rate against cumulative production in the regression objective. It then compares hyperbolic, Duong, and power-law exponential fits side by side to bracket an EUR range and exports the results in an Aries-compatible format [tPB4O0ryZww @ 00:03:47].

Where the curve ends is an economics question, not a geology one. TopDogEngineer defines breakeven as oil rate times oil price, plus oil rate times GOR times gas price, minus operating cost, equals zero. He derives GOR from the derivative of cumulative gas with respect to cumulative oil, substitutes the Arps cumulative equation, and solves with Excel Solver [4mzbNb16NQc @ 00:03:24]. He starts from a $3.35 gas price, multiplies it by a 7/8 NRI, and subtracts severance and ad valorem taxes, for a net of about $2.067 per Mcf. The run lands on an economic rate of 140.3 bbl/month; below that rate, in his words, 'we're losing money' [4mzbNb16NQc @ 00:08:25]. Mergers & Inquisitions builds the forward model in Excel. Inputs are a 10 MMcfe/d IP, a 60% initial decline, and a hyperbolic formula with a log-based D factor. Decline is set to MAX(formula, terminal) so it never drops below 5%. Production is set to MIN(prior production times one minus decline, EUR minus cumulative), for a total of 14.25 Bcfe [2tJpxiIqFSM @ 00:06:44]. With $4.7M of D&C capex, his version produced a 113% IRR and a $15M NPV10. The company's own figures were 124% and $6.3M, and he attributes the gap to a different curve shape [2tJpxiIqFSM @ 00:15:17]. A different bend gives a very different answer.

The royalty-side arithmetic is just as mechanical. Mr. Business walks through a check. Ten net mineral acres in a 640-acre unit is 1.5625%; at a 20% royalty, that gives a 0.3125% NRI. Ninety thousand barrels at $70 grosses $6.3M, so the owner receives about $19,700, or roughly $18,500 after an assumed 5-6% in combined taxes [8gaFGCKNpnk @ 00:07:11]. Applying his decline of 90k, 48k, 35k, 28k, and 24k barrels, five years total about $49k gross, with more than 40% of it in year one. Matt Sands gives a shortcut for mature producing assets: average the last three months of royalty and multiply by 50-70x, or up to 100x in hot areas. He prices a full engineering valuation at 2-4 hours of work, about $400-800 [86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:29:36]. In his example, a $10-15k per acre offer on 5 acres might really be worth $20-30k per acre. ComboCurve screened the Haynesville down to 2,022 wells that passed its vintage, lateral, proppant, and production filters. The medians were a b of 0.94, a Di of 59, payout in 19 months at flat $70/$3.25, an NPV10 of $5.8 million, and an IRR of 52% [k4f-XlIpXZU @ 00:19:20]. Those medians are benchmarks a buyer's offer can be measured against before anyone signs.

callout.title: Clean the Fit Before You Trust Any Number
callout.body: The curve is only as good as the data window and constraints behind it. These are the settings and checks the practitioners apply before a forecast reaches a valuation.
items: Use the First decline start method for capacity-limited, choked gas wells instead of the default Max start [Danomics — gleafhkBQWg @ 00:03:04]
Move the start-time marker to exclude early flowback data before running any hyperbolic regression [KAPPA Engineering — tPB4O0ryZww @ 00:01:54]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Troy W. Eckard of Eckard Enterprises frames steep shale decline as a gift. Wells that once crawled along at 50 to 100 BOE per day now open at high rates, and operators target payback inside 36 months. Eckard tells owners it is not a negative that wells decline but a positive that they start so high, with wells predicted to last 50 to 75 years after the hyperbolic leveling-off [nn1juJ3_-WA @ 00:10:01]. Mr. Business runs the same numbers colder. In their five-year example, more than 45% of total royalty income lands in year one and first-year decline runs 60 to 70%, so the operating rule is that a royalty is not a salary but a depleting asset [hIerB5MQ52U @ 00:12:19]. Steven Hatcher splits the difference for sellers. Peak value sits in the months right after first production, because a shale well recovers 70 to 80% of its volume in its first two years, while a pre-production sale trades a lower price for dumping development risk on the buyer [CiR-w5lHfvI @ 00:11:46]. Matt Sands lands on the opposite side of the sell trigger: hold unless the cash is needed now, and when it is, carve out an NPRI or sell any slice from 1% to 100% rather than the whole estate [86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:31:06].

With no Zillow for minerals and most sale prices undisclosed, Justin Williams, the West Texas inheritor on Matt Sands' show, calls the market approach the preferred method. Pull arm's-length comps from auction sites like EnergyNet and normalize everything to price per net mineral acre, the mineral version of price per square foot [86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:13:00]. Sands pushes back hard. Auction fever makes bidders overpay or underpay, a credible comp set needs 50-plus transactions inside about six months in one tight area, and geology and 3D seismic can swing prices between neighboring townships, so auction data gets taken with a grain of salt [86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:13:25]. The rival playbook is the income or engineering approach: pick analog wells, adjust them for one- or two-mile laterals, build a type curve, layer in spacing and timing, then compute NPV. Sands puts that at a two-to-four-hour job that runs about $400 to $800 [86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:15:30]. Mr. Business sides with the engineering camp for producing royalty. Professionals value with decline curve analysis and PV10, undrilled locations get discounted, stripper wells can be shut in or plugged, and a $2,000 check from a six-month-old well overstates future income [8gaFGCKNpnk @ 00:12:28].

On curve mechanics, Matt Sands flags an open split in type-curve building. One camp fits a single curve to the averaged production of analog wells from the last ten years, normalized for lateral length and time. The other fits every well individually and then averages the results [VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:28:42]. Danomics runs the per-well style at scale, auto-declining about 4,000 wells in seconds with b capped at 1.3 and qi capped at twice the maximum observed rate, while openly refusing to call 1.3 the correct value [gleafhkBQWg @ 00:04:04]. KAPPA Engineering refuses to bet on a single equation. It excludes early flowback, weights rate against cumulative production in the regression objective, then stacks hyperbolic, Duong and power-law exponential fits on the same well and compares them to bracket a range of EURs [tPB4O0ryZww @ 00:03:47]. Ryan Hassen of whitson attacks the premise that analogs transfer cleanly. Across more than 100,000 wells, lateral length behaves close to 'a shale is a shale,' but frac fluid intensity, water cut and spacing are special snowflakes. Eagle Ford shows the tightest depletion contour and the Delaware Third Bone Spring Sand the widest [qdJuFyTh5yU @ 00:02:33].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is the paycheck itself. Troy W. Eckard warns that the first royalty check arrives about six months after production starts and bundles one to five months of volume. The next check covers a single month, so it can come in at a third or a sixth of the first. Eckard's instruction is not to be alarmed but grateful for revenue captured fast [nn1juJ3_-WA @ 00:08:21]. Mr. Business hammers a second gap: real checks are always lower than the headline math. Regional differentials pull a $70 WTI print down to a realized $66 to $68, and post-production costs, 'cost-free' lease language fights and severance taxes chew on the rest [hIerB5MQ52U @ 00:11:07]. On gas, the same channel says deductions hinge on exact lease wording such as 'free of costs,' 'market value at the well' or 'proceeds received,' plus state law [8gaFGCKNpnk @ 00:15:08]. Then the buyers circle. Matt Sands states flatly that buyers will offer less than value, and pairs that with a data rule: 18 to 24 months of unrestricted production before trusting any curve, since curtailment, waterfloods and CO2 projects sit outside the standard fit [VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:34:47].

Model risk shows up in the inputs before it shows up in the checks. Ryan Hassen found that one apparent wellbore-azimuth anomaly was just a wrong EPSG code, and warns that if a GOR map is garbage, no machine-learned relationship can save the forecast. The 100,000-well dataset also carries selection bias, because it covers only shales that worked [qdJuFyTh5yU @ 00:12:19]. Mergers & Inquisitions built a hyperbolic type curve in Excel from a 10 MMcfe/d IP, a 60% initial decline and a 5% terminal floor. It landed at a 113% IRR and $15 million NPV10, against Silver Bow's published 124% and $6.3 million, a gap the instructor pins on curve shape [2tJpxiIqFSM @ 00:15:17]. Worse, issuers like Range Resources disclose EUR and D&C cost but no equation. That forces a goal-seeked 4 to 5% decline over roughly 25 years against a reserve life near 20, which the instructor calls a very common issue [2tJpxiIqFSM @ 00:18:02]. Francis Ramos II adds a diagnostic check before any exponential math. Rate versus cumulative must plot linear, and semi-log rate versus time must run as a straight line, while a plain linear rate-versus-time chart does not reveal whether decline is exponential [u3kTgNXLIGI @ 00:02:47].

Every forecast ends at an economic wall. TopDogEngineer solves for it directly, setting oil revenue plus GOR-linked gas revenue minus operating cost to zero. In their Excel case the economic rate lands at 140.3 bbl per month; below it the well is losing money, and drilling and completion cost is pushed out to the NPV step [4mzbNb16NQc @ 00:08:49]. The Crude Files notes that about three in four US wells already produce under 15 bbl per day. Plugging and abandonment costs run from tens of thousands upward, and orphan wells often land on taxpayers and states [R-AasPj-Y5E @ 00:13:06]. Price can drag the wall forward. The Crude Files sets a Dallas Fed breakeven near $65 against 2025 oil in the low-to-mid $60s. ComboCurve reports core Haynesville gas not even at break-even, with JP Morgan's roughly $3.50 core breakeven against about $3 gas [k4f-XlIpXZU @ 00:05:53]. Permian Resources shows the defensive play. With Waha falling to negative $9.52, it choked back about 20% of gas by curtailing high-GOR wells and used already-paid firm transport to realize a positive $0.38 per Mcf, an estimated $75 million uplift [Kwv0e2yhRmA @ 00:08:47].

callout.title: Four Checks Before Pricing, Budgeting or Selling a Royalty
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a trap practitioners hit or watched owners hit: inflated first checks, curves fit to bad data, garbage inputs, and irreversible sales.
items: Do not budget off the first check: it covers one to five months of production, and the next single-month check can run a third or a sixth of it [Eckard Enterprises | Oil & Gas Investing — nn1juJ3_-WA @ 00:08:21].
No forecast without 18 to 24 months of unrestricted production; curtailed, waterflooded or CO2 wells break standard decline curve analysis [Matt Sands — VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:35:19].
Audit the inputs before the model: a wrong EPSG code faked an azimuth signal, and a garbage GOR map wrecks any forecast [Whitson Academy — qdJuFyTh5yU @ 00:12:19].
Before any sale, pay for your own deed review, because buyer-drafted deeds can sweep in suspense or escheated funds, and a 100% sale is a done deal [Matt Sands — 86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:27:15].

chapters.pull_quote: "The smart way to think about a royalty is not as a salary, it's as a depleting asset." — Mr. Business (hIerB5MQ52U @ 00:12:19).
action_checklist: Pull permits and wells by legal description from the state oil and gas commission map, and classify the minerals as producing or non-producing [Matt Sands — 86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:09:22].
Compute decimal interest as net mineral acres over unit acres times royalty rate; 10 NMA in a 640-acre unit at 20% gives 0.3125% [Mr. Business — 8gaFGCKNpnk @ 00:07:11].
Fit a two-part curve on a semi-log plot: hyperbolic first, then exponential terminal decline at 8% to 15% per year [Matt Sands — VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:21:29].
Export Well Database production to Excel, keep b under 1.3, set 8% terminal decline, and multiply by your decimal interest [Matt Sands — VYytHJ0lMVw @ 00:39:28].
Solve for the economic rate where oil revenue plus gas revenue minus operating cost equals zero, using Excel Solver or any root finder [TopDogEngineer — 4mzbNb16NQc @ 00:03:24].
Cross-check mature producing assets by averaging the last three months of royalty and multiplying by 50 to 70, up to 100 in hot areas [Matt Sands — 86mQK92f7Bg @ 00:29:36].

chapters.question_prompt: How do I buy or sell mineral rights profitably, and how do I protect myself from bad buyers?
chapters.title: Buying and Selling Mineral Rights
chapters.subtitle: Reasons to sell, three ways to sell, types of mineral buyers and who to avoid, the history of mineral buying, selling at peak value, buying producing cash-flowing minerals, brokering and flipping vs. holding royalties, and building monthly income
chapters.executive_summary: Mineral buyers and sell-side advisors converge on one rule: follow the drill bit. Steven Hatcher, Troy Eckard and Matt Sands all buy proven, multi-zone acreage near active permits, chain title from patent to present because no title company insures minerals, and treat a sale as a liquidity trade where the seller hands price and volume risk to the buyer. The mechanics are numeric: Sands discounts producing minerals at about 10%, rig-on-site acreage at 15-20% and five-year-plan acreage at 20-30%, and pays 36-60x monthly royalty for old flat wells; Hatcher reports a $95,000 PDP buy recouping 40% in nine months and a $30,000-plus contract flip with no capital. Disagreements center on never-sell advice, dry gas, auction quality, and whether flipping minerals is a legitimate play or something to avoid.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The buyers agree on one thing first: follow the drill bit. Steven Hatcher calls West Texas 'Mecca,' adds North Louisiana, North Dakota and Northeastern Colorado, and tells buyers to stay near active permitting and drilling [I-uVEypiL9w @ 00:02:32]. He backs that with his own allocation: 95% of drilling is horizontal shale, he spends 95% of his time there, and buying in the wrong area is the first mistake on his list [zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:04:32]. Matt Sands gives the same instruction in distance terms: buy one to two miles from active drilling that is moving your way, because even undrilled acreage in that path may get leased, and a rig running 16 horizontal wells means royalties inside 12 months [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:27:56]. Troy Eckard tightens the screen further. He refuses speculative minerals, wants well-drilled direct offsets that are proven and derisked, and wants primary, secondary and tertiary zones stacked underneath, because a single-zone tract depletes to no residual value [S-yENwSQhi0 @ 00:01:11]. The shared logic is that operators spend millions per well, so the mineral owner's only job is to sit where a well-capitalized company is already committing capital. Sands calls anything outside that zone a goat pasture and warns that minerals are not a lottery ticket.

The second point of agreement is that the asset is invisible until you dig it out of the courthouse. Hatcher notes the surface owner is usually not the mineral owner, because minerals get reserved when surface sells, so he chains title through county deed records and grantor/grantee indexes, mostly online, using mineral tax rolls in Texas and pooling and unitization records in Oklahoma and Ohio [I-uVEypiL9w @ 00:03:48]. Sands states flatly that no title company will underwrite title insurance on minerals, so the buyer must run title from patent to present, and he warns that 640 gross acres can shrink to a quarter of a net acre once fractions are traced [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:16:39]. In his Cashflow Ninja walkthrough he pulls the oil-and-gas commission's list of interested parties for each drilling unit, verifies deeds at the county clerk, and corroborates ownership with operator title opinions and royalty checks because fraudulent deeds circulate [uhffuS4DlLQ @ 00:33:33]. Hatcher reduces the whole discipline to one line: you have to learn how to run title and review revenue statements to understand exactly what they own, and 'that is the entire game right there' [zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:05:42]. Finding hidden ownership and underwriting are precisely the two gaps he tells wholesalers and land flippers they must close.

Buyers and sell-side advisors also agree on what the transaction actually is: a liquidity trade. Hatcher frames his company's role as providing a valuable service, liquidity, to owners who want to buy a home, start a business, retire or move into more stable assets, and he likens selling to taking the lower Powerball lump sum over the bigger 30-year stream [WvlIfeyW4-Q @ 00:02:52]. In his seller-side video he spells out what changes hands: the seller shifts price risk and volume risk onto the buyer in exchange for certainty in a fixed sum, and selling half or a quarter is allowed [Sz-1-E8zTqU @ 00:05:01]. Sands rejects blanket never-sell advice on the same grounds, telling concentrated owners they can sell any fraction, such as half, and diversify by tract, basin or oil-versus-gas mix [y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:13:51]. Daniel Lewis pitches Oklahoma owners the identical flexibility, buying anything from 5 to 50,000 net mineral acres with partial sales welcome and no pressure [qZGXdB7E1lE @ 00:01:45]. For an acquirer, that consensus becomes the opening line of every call: you are not asking for the whole estate, only the slice that pays off a mortgage, a medical bill or a wedding.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Valuation starts from Hatcher's warning that there is no Zillow or Redfin for minerals, so he prices off three methods: a multiple of the existing royalty check, price per acre from comps, and discounted cash flow [I-uVEypiL9w @ 00:04:36]. Sands supplies the discount rates that drive the DCF: about 10% for producing minerals, 15-20% with a rig on site, and 20-30% for acreage inside an operator's SEC five-year plan within one to two miles of drilling. His shortcut for wells older than five years with no future development is 36 to 60 times the monthly royalty [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:33:41]. On the sell side he reports how buyers haircut the price deck: at $100 oil they underwrite at $75-80, at roughly $60 oil they underwrite near $50, and they apply a 10-15% discount rate, which makes commodity price timing and development timing the two biggest levers on value [y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:23:04]. In his tips episode he explains why wellbore-only interests are in hot demand: PDP gets discounted at 8-10% against 30-50% for PUD, because producing wells demand a lower discount rate, which means higher value [RR2BlQf14H8 @ 00:20:22]. Offers are typically quoted per net mineral acre, such as three thousand dollars per acre.

Deal flow is a records-and-outreach machine. Sands points to statutory pooling filings, such as those at the Oklahoma Corporation Commission, which list mineral owners a year or more before permits appear, and he runs the same outreach land investors use: letters, calls, email and texts, timed to catch owners facing something like medical bills [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:29:35]. Hatcher's sourcing system is four moves: track operator permits, pull tax, regulatory and courthouse records, contact owners systematically, and buy only where operators are spending [zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:05:42]. Blue Mesa Minerals warns that starting an acquisitions company is a lot of work built on two numbers games, because many owners must be contacted to find one seller [08zWLxyGaag @ 00:02:20]. Sands sequences the paper so cash stays protected: target permitted or drilling acreage, pull the commission's interested-parties list, verify deeds, send offers, run DCF at your target return, and only after a signed purchase and sale agreement hire a landman, then adjust price to the net acres found, close, and notify the operator promptly [uhffuS4DlLQ @ 00:34:38]. He also notes that one winner pays for three or four duds, which is why he calls the whole business a numbers game.

Hatcher puts hard numbers on three ways to make money. For PDP cash flow, he paid $95,000 for 16 Louisiana acres with two existing and two new Haynesville wells, recouped 40% in nine months, and projects about $155,000 total, a 1.63 MOIC and 20% IRR [zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:01:54]. For white-space appreciation, 60 acres in Benville Parish cost $325,000; nine months later the operator permitted and drilled four wells, and he projects over $1 million, a 3x return. For brokering, he contracted an Ohio interest at $220,000 after courthouse title revealed more acreage than the 5.5 acres on the tax records, then assigned it for $250,000, netting over $30,000 with no capital used [zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:03:32]. Sands calibrates entry pricing: owning 1/160 of a 160-acre tract equals one net mineral acre worth a few thousand dollars, beginners can start with quarter-acre deals costing a few hundred, but in the Permian owners get unsolicited $25,000-per-acre offers and a $5,000 bid gets laughed out [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:13:06]. On the sell side he quotes non-producing Permian at $5,000-10,000 per net royalty acre, possibly two to three times that once permitted, versus a couple hundred per acre for an Oklahoma goat pasture [y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:30:45].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether to sell at all. Steven Hatcher rejects the never-sell mindset outright, telling owners to treat minerals as a balance-sheet asset and weigh the opportunity cost of holding against the opportunity cost of selling [Sz-1-E8zTqU @ 00:00:35]. Hatcher frames a sale through the Powerball choice: $500M paid over 30 years versus a $300M lump sum, where selling means choosing the lower lump sum in exchange for certainty [WvlIfeyW4-Q @ 00:03:22]. Matt Sands lands on the same side, disagreeing with blanket never-sell advice and stressing that any fraction, such as half, can go to market while the rest keeps paying [y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:13:51]. Yet in the 2020 outlook episode with guest Justin Williams, the counterweight surfaces: buyers were calling that moment a good buying opportunity, so an owner selling into the window risks handing future upside to the buyer [RR2BlQf14H8 @ 00:33:07]. Both camps treat the asset as a tradeable position rather than a family heirloom; they diverge on timing. Hatcher sells certainty and redeployment into a home, 1031 real estate, a farm tract, or a small business, while Sands asks a harder question first: is the buyer bidding into a trough that will reverse?

Commodity and basin selection split the room just as hard. Troy Eckard avoids dry gas, naming the Marcellus and Haynesville, and only breaks that rule for a pure rate-of-return play under a solid operator targeting 1.5 to 3x [S-yENwSQhi0 @ 00:03:35]. Steven Hatcher walked straight into Haynesville gas anyway: 16 acres in Bojer Parish, Louisiana with two existing and two new wells, bought for $95,000, 40% recouped in nine months, projected at roughly $155,000 total for a 1.63 MOIC and 20% IRR, which lands inside Eckard's own exception band [zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:01:54]. Matt Sands goes further on gas, arguing that US gas at $2.50 to $3 per Mcf reflects a glut and that LNG export capacity coming online points to buying depressed gas assets now [uhffuS4DlLQ @ 00:26:17]. On geography, Hatcher calls West Texas 'Mecca' and says to buy near permitting and drilling [I-uVEypiL9w @ 00:02:32], while Sands steers toward overlooked areas under regulatory pressure because the Permian costs multiples per acre and draws more competition. Pick the lane deliberately: Eckard's legacy-hold filter demands multiple stacked formations, Hatcher's filter is the right neighborhood, right operator and multiple wells, and Sands insists on a mix of oil and gas across basins.

Auctions and flipping draw the most direct contradictions. On the buy side, Blue Mesa Minerals reports seeing decent deals at auction but never really good ones, since lots have usually been passed over by everybody first [08zWLxyGaag @ 00:01:17]. From the sell side, Matt Sands flips the read: auction commissions run 6 to 10%, but less sophisticated auction buyers may overpay, and Sands positions a fixed, lower advisory percentage as the alternative route to competing bids [y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:34:41]. Steven Hatcher teaches flipping as a core income stream: a Harrison County, Ohio deal started at 5.5 acres off tax records, courthouse title turned up more acreage, and the contract at $220,000 was assigned for $250,000, netting over 30K with no capital deployed [zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:03:32]. Blue Mesa Minerals rejects that model on its own book, describing flippers who buy, wait for a new well, then list on EnergyNet, and stating it keeps everything it buys [vogFrTHuYiY @ 00:09:12]. The two flips are different animals: Hatcher's is a contract assignment with zero capital at risk, while the Blue Mesa complaint targets buy-and-hold-for-a-well arbitrage aimed at auction buyers who miss the coming decline. Sellers should know which flipper is on the other side of the table.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Title is where practitioners have already watched real money disappear. The Modern Land Investor host spent roughly $3,000 to $4,000 on a mineral-rights attorney to learn severance, parked the severed minerals in a separate entity without researching them, and never earned a dime from them [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:02:33]. Matt Sands spells out why diligence is non-negotiable on that same episode: no title company will insure minerals, title runs from patent to present, 640 gross acres can shrink to a quarter net acre, and a $6,000 quiet-title suit on a quarter NMA means pass or pay very little [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:57:36]. On Cashflow Ninja, Sands adds fraudulent deeds to the threat list and corroborates every claimed ownership interest against operator title opinions and actual royalty checks [uhffuS4DlLQ @ 00:30:04]. For sellers, the same defects cut the other way: in MRP 310 Sands reports that defects lower offers, cures such as a determination of heirship or reopened probate sit on the critical path to closing, and sellers can negotiate a split of the curative cost [y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:20:51]. Run title before money moves, or price every defect directly into the offer.

The second failure cluster is development that never arrives or decays faster than modeled. Troy Eckard warns that a single-zone position leaves no residual value once it depletes, and that an undercapitalized 'Johnny come lately' operator may wait about two years for each well to pay out, stretching four to twelve analog wells across 10 to 20 years [S-yENwSQhi0 @ 00:02:19]. Matt Sands flags that operators may never drill permitted wells and that new wells can underperform the analogs used to price them, so the fix is diversification across states, basins and commodities [uhffuS4DlLQ @ 00:27:16]. On Modern Land Investor, Sands adds that an oil-price crash can cancel drilling plans outright, that a property where nothing will happen is a 'goat pasture,' and that one winner has to pay for three or four duds [1c2UBDuXhrk @ 00:31:45]. Blue Mesa Minerals quantifies the decline trap from the auction desk: a new well's revenue can fall to maybe 10% within a year, and $1,000 a month can become $200 a year later [vogFrTHuYiY @ 00:07:40]. Any buyer underwriting off a first-month check without a decline curve is paying peak price for a fading stream.

The final cluster is the paper itself. Steven Hatcher tells owners to throw away unsolicited mail resembling a check, legal agreement or deed, notes that sending deed-like mailers is illegal in several jurisdictions, and lists evasive identity, no online presence and high-pressure tactics as red flags [WIqkczvqoz0 @ 00:06:12]. The MRP 70 episode with Justin Williams warns that buyers forced to make assumptions will make them in their own favor, which is why an independent consultant or engineer at $600 to $800 per property is pitched as the way to level the playing field [RR2BlQf14H8 @ 00:06:55]. MRP 310 puts the PSA risk bluntly, 'it takes one sentence, Matt, to sign away far more than what you were anticipating,' with royalties in suspense the named target, and Sands adds that leasing at 12% instead of 25% in Reeves, Lea or Eddy counties halves the property's value before any sale [y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:21:04]. Blue Mesa Minerals closes the loop: no escrow companies will go near mineral rights, so the sale is a signed deed against a wire in a 'Wild Wild West' market, and Sands separately insists on getting paid before handing over the deed [vogFrTHuYiY @ 00:02:21].

callout.title: Pre-Close Kill Switches
callout.body: Stop the deal if any of these practitioner-reported traps is live on either side of the table.
items: Do not spend on a landman until a signed purchase and sale agreement is in hand, then adjust price to the net acres actually found [Cashflow Ninja — uhffuS4DlLQ @ 00:34:38].

Have the PSA reviewed for any sentence that signs over royalties in suspense before signing anything [Matt Sands — y5etlsUEcO0 @ 00:21:34].
Run title and review revenue statements before buying, because there are 101 ways to lose your ass on an oil and gas deal [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — zV7XrUzBPJQ @ 00:05:07].

Vet every buyer by first name, last name and city in a Google search, and confirm the company site shows owners, officers, funding and a physical address [Steven Hatcher | Minerals Guy — WIqkczvqoz0 @ 00:03:04].
Collect multiple bids and play them off each other, using Voss's Never Split the Difference as the negotiation playbook [Matt Sands — RR2BlQf14H8 @ 00:36:28].

chapters.question_prompt: What tax benefits apply to royalty and working-interest owners, and how do I pass minerals to heirs?
chapters.title: Taxes, Working Interests and Passing Minerals to Heirs
chapters.subtitle: Percentage and cost depletion, intangible drilling cost deductions, working vs. royalty interest risk and tax treatment, property taxes on minerals, tax strategies for royalty owners, inheritance issues, affidavits of heirship, and family wealth transfer
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree on the split that drives every tax and inheritance decision. Royalty owners pay no drilling costs and shelter 15% of gross royalties through percentage depletion. Working interest owners fund wells and write off 65-85% of the ticket as intangible drilling costs against ordinary income. The street mechanics run through Schedule E depletion lines, a tax ID on file with every operator to stop roughly 30% withholding, cost-depletion appraisals costing a couple thousand dollars, and Texas affidavits of heirship recorded in every county to release suspended royalties. The disagreements are sharp. IDC percentages range from 65-80% up to 100%, royalty 1031 eligibility is contested, and working interest reporting splits between K-1 and Schedule C. Troy Eckard calls drilling mandatory above $300-500K of income, while Tracy Lenz says non-op owners are stuck in the middle.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner draws the same first line: a royalty owner carries no drilling bill, while a working interest owner pays the freight. Tracy Lenz, a petroleum engineer and independent appraiser, explains that a royalty owner pays only when paid. Ad valorem tax, severance tax and marketing fees come off the check, and if a well goes negative, the shortfall is netted against future royalties instead of billed out [mHolW0RfGQ0 @ 00:01:03]. On a standard lease the operator takes 80% of revenue while paying 100% of costs. Lenz describes it as the operator 'paying a dollar in order to make 80 cents,' with the royalty share running 20%, 25%, or 18% down to 12% [mHolW0RfGQ0 @ 00:02:42]. Mike of Sovereign Energy Partners reduces the decision to two variables: who pays the costs and who gets what share. He models a 10% working interest in a $1M well that costs $100K, against a royalty position with no capital calls that he calls 'a much more passive form of participation' [J9jZGFyolV0 @ 00:03:26]. Tim Pawul goes further, calling minerals a 'triple net lease of oil and gas' with no ongoing CapEx once they are purchased or inherited [mcQ5KsrbKzc @ 00:05:11]. Matt Sands confirms that royalty owners bear only severance and property taxes plus post-production costs [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:07:58].

The second point of agreement is percentage depletion. Austin at ADKF says the rate is 'typically... 15% of your gross income.' The deduction is unavailable in a net-loss year and is capped at 65% of net income. The IRS lets you take the higher of cost or percentage depletion, never both [GPDm8NftR5U @ 00:00:51]. Lenz walks through the same 15%: $10,000 in 1099-MISC Box 2 yields a $1,500 deduction, leaving 85% taxable. Royalty, mineral, ORRI and working interest owners all qualify [NYvxAlVlAmQ @ 00:23:24]. Lenz describes depletion as a tax write-off 'for you owning less things.' Matt Sands and Justin Williams add the ceiling: the deduction is limited to the smaller of 100% of taxable income from the property or 65% of taxable income from all sources. It also runs against royalties only, never against a lease bonus payment [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:11:58]. On the working interest side, Scott, a Colorado tax lawyer at Protect Wealth Academy, names the big three: tangible drilling costs, intangible drilling costs and depletion. He classes working interest as active income that offsets W-2 wages, while royalties stay passive [J21M9DVmwY8 @ 00:22:26]. The shared operator read is that royalties shelter 15% of the check, while working interests shelter most of the drilling budget itself in year one.

On passing minerals to heirs, the consensus is that paperwork, not tax, is where families lose money. Sands and Williams treat minerals as real property conveyed by deed, 'very similar to conveying a house.' They warn that operators park royalties in suspense until heirship is settled, which they call 'a headache' costing 'several thousand dollar usually in each state' [cO3OBCezwjw @ 00:10:28]. Royalty Clerk's Texas walkthrough opens on exactly that freeze. Walt died three years ago without a will, the checks stopped, and Texas law lets the operator hold royalties without interest while ownership is in reasonable doubt [q5XqULtWaUQ @ 00:00:57]. Pawul lists funds in suspense among the costliest owner mistakes and cites one $10M recovery [mcQ5KsrbKzc @ 00:44:56]. On tax, the speakers agree that inheritance itself triggers no tax that year. The value at the date of death or the alternate valuation date becomes the basis for any later sale, and Sands reports fielding one to two inheritance questions per week [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:04:12]. The same baseline prerequisites recur across channels: know every county where the interest sits, keep a tax ID on file with each operator, and leave heirs the deeds, leases, well lists, check stubs and division orders they will need.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Working interest math starts with the intangible drilling cost bucket. Scott puts IDC at 70-85% of well costs, with small producers reaching 100% and large ones limited to 70%. On a $50K ticket, 85% IDC saves about $16K and bonus depreciation on the $7,500 remainder saves about $3K, for roughly $18,500, or 37%, back [J21M9DVmwY8 @ 00:24:11]. Neil Jesani Tax Advisors runs the same split at 65-80% IDC with the remainder depreciable. The firm quotes bonus depreciation at 40% for 2025 and uses an example of $80K IDC plus $20K depreciable [FagQvbKX71g @ 00:01:05]. Toby Mathis prices the year-one deduction at 70-75%, up to 80%, which turns a $100K investment into about a $70K deduction worth '20-something thousand.' Mathis also flags a 90-day rule: drilling must start within 90 days of year-end to deduct in the year invested [TfG5auc0OXc @ 00:06:17]. Troy Eckard pitches the most aggressive version. Eckard claims that under the 'OBBB,' 100% of the amount invested comes off gross income, so a $2M earner who puts in $1M shows $1M taxable, and that the write-offs are identical for a dry hole and a producer [41VgsNOdrto @ 00:04:57]. Scott's counterweight is that IDC is recaptured as ordinary income on sale, though the time value of money still favors taking the deduction.

For royalty owners, the filing mechanics are specific. Lenz places percentage depletion on Schedule E Part 1: property code 6 on line 1b, income on line 4 and depletion on line 18. 'Gross' means before severance and post-production costs such as gathering, marketing, transportation, processing and fuel. Lease bonuses, advance royalties and easements are excluded [NYvxAlVlAmQ @ 00:32:53]. Lenz's cost depletion formula is basis divided by barrels remaining, times barrels sold, with a switch point around $9-10 per barrel. The 15% rate applies up to 1,000 bbl/day, using a 6:1 BOE conversion [NYvxAlVlAmQ @ 00:39:29]. Sands passes along a listener-CPA tip: an inherited step-up can accelerate cost depletion. The appraisal and EUR it requires cost 'a couple thousand dollars,' though, so it only pays on a substantial interest [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:14:19]. Cash management is the other lever. Without a W-9 or tax ID on file, operators withhold about 30% by law. Once the tax ID is in, nothing is withheld, so owners have to save cash and make estimated payments to avoid penalties [_MHogbd2xzU @ 00:16:53]. Ad valorem bills vary by state: Colorado taxes severed non-producing minerals at about $3-$5 a year, while Texas sends a bill only once a well starts producing.

The heir-side execution is a paperwork sprint. Royalty Clerk lays out the Texas affidavit of heirship, a sworn, notarized statement on the Estates Code §203.002 form. It lists the date of death, every marriage and how it ended, every child living or dead, and whether a will exists. It should ideally be signed by a disinterested neighbor, friend or pastor (operators often want two) and recorded with the county clerk in every county holding minerals [q5XqULtWaUQ @ 00:03:05]. The packet to each company is the recorded affidavit, a certified death certificate, and each heir's address and W-9. It goes with two written questions: what else is needed, and how much has been held [q5XqULtWaUQ @ 00:04:03]. Sands and Williams push structure upstream. A properly funded trust avoids probate, and a family LLC changes ownership without recording a deed. Keeping interests whole in a trust or LLC beats fractionalizing from 100% to 50%, 25%, 12.5% and 6.25% [cO3OBCezwjw @ 00:08:09]. On sale, Sands sets the hold at a year and a day for long-term treatment. An appraisal pays when the inheritance was within 10 years and proceeds reach multiple six figures. Sands cites the 2023 estate exemption at $13.61M per individual, scheduled to sunset at the end of 2025 [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:27:40].

callout.title: Depletion and filing moves the practitioners use
callout.body: Four execution edges, drawn from the speakers' own filing and depletion workflows, that most owners leave on the table.
items: Mix depletion methods property by property. Lenz says you do not have to use the same method for each property, so you can run cost depletion on a freshly inherited asset with newly drilled wells and percentage depletion elsewhere [Tracy Lenz — NYvxAlVlAmQ @ 00:22:40].
Percentage depletion keeps running after basis hits zero ('It doesn't stop when your basis is gone'), while cost depletion stops at zero [Tracy Lenz — NYvxAlVlAmQ @ 00:46:35].
Deduct the paper chase. Attorney deed filings, landman research and consulting fees are deductible, so keep every receipt [Matt Sands — z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:09:45].
Plan for late K-1s on working interests. They arrive in June or July, so file an extension rather than filing short [Protect Wealth Academy — J21M9DVmwY8 @ 00:45:00].

sop_steps.title: Inventory every interest and county
sop_steps.action: Pull check stubs, 1099s, county mineral rolls and unclaimed property records, then search '[county] CAD' for each county.
sop_steps.detail: Royalty Clerk's checklist is stubs, 1099s, county mineral rolls and unclaimed property under the decedent's name [Royalty Clerk — q5XqULtWaUQ @ 00:05:02]. Sands and Williams use county CAD lookups, noting that Texas counties share one platform [Matt Sands — _MHogbd2xzU @ 00:12:51].

sop_steps.title: Lock in tax ID and cash reserves
sop_steps.action: Send a W-9 to every operator, then set aside cash and make estimated payments on the unwithheld royalties.
sop_steps.detail: Once a tax ID is provided, the operator withholds no income tax from royalty payments, so the owner must save cash and pay estimates to avoid a penalty [Matt Sands — z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:06:35].

sop_steps.title: Pick the depletion method per property
sop_steps.action: Default to 15% percentage depletion, and commission an appraisal for cost depletion only on substantial inherited interests.
sop_steps.detail: You take the higher of the two methods, never both [ADKF | With You All The Way — GPDm8NftR5U @ 00:03:05]. Sands says a cost-depletion appraisal runs a couple thousand dollars and only makes sense on a substantial interest [Matt Sands — z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:14:19].

sop_steps.title: Record heirship and claim suspense
sop_steps.action: Record the affidavit of heirship in every mineral county, send each operator the full packet, and demand all held funds.
sop_steps.detail: Record with the county clerk in every county where minerals sit, then send each company the packet [Royalty Clerk — q5XqULtWaUQ @ 00:03:43]. Once the papers are accepted, ask for all of the suspended money [Royalty Clerk — q5XqULtWaUQ @ 00:04:20].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether an outsider should ever hold a non-operated working interest. Tracy Lenz, a petroleum engineer and independent appraiser, argues that the two best seats are royalty owner or operator. In Lenz's view the non-op owner is stuck in the middle, with no control over spending or timing, and working interest is only worth chasing for industry insiders such as part-time landmen [mHolW0RfGQ0 @ 00:08:06]. Troy Eckard flips that completely. Eckard tells physicians that anyone making over $300,000 to $500,000 a year who is not drilling wells is making a massive mistake, and pitches nearly 100 wells in six years with zero dry holes and roughly 93% of capital back in under two years [41VgsNOdrto @ 00:24:04]. Mike at Sovereign Energy Partners refuses to crown a winner. Neither structure is inherently better, Mike says, and the playbook is to pair working interest for upside with royalty interest as the lower-risk income base, matched to risk tolerance and investment mindset [J9jZGFyolV0 @ 00:05:35]. Scott, a Colorado tax lawyer, cuts against the deduction-driven pitch entirely with a blunt rule: don't invest for the tax benefits. The operator and the deal still have to stand on their own [J21M9DVmwY8 @ 00:40:42].

The 1031 exchange is the most direct factual collision in this chapter. Scott states that royalty and leasehold interests do not qualify, that eligibility turns on state law treating the interest as real property, and that royalty holders should not plan on a 1031 exchange on the back end [J21M9DVmwY8 @ 00:33:58]. Chris Bentley of Bellator, who runs $28 million of Permian royalties, says the opposite. Exchanges run both directions between mineral rights and commercial real estate through a qualified intermediary, and Bentley asks why an investor would not 1031 into a portfolio of mineral interests that pays every month [Ij8eFGyDOC4 @ 00:09:19]. Matt Sands sides with Bentley on the sell side, naming a 1031 into a rental property as a way to defer gains after selling inherited minerals [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:30:35]. Tim Pawul threads the needle with four routes. The first is a minerals DST such as Montego Minerals or Resource Royalty. The second is the 'lazy man's 1031': the seller eats the capital gain and buys into a non-op IDC fund with a GP flip, for roughly a 90% year-one write-off. The other two are public royalty trusts and a direct asset. Pawul warns that you typically cannot 1031 into a fund, and when Pawul's own father sold, the IDC fund won [mcQ5KsrbKzc @ 00:16:14].

Depletion method is the next fork. Austin at ADKF says royalty holders and other passive investors typically default to percentage depletion because it is easier. The IRS lets you take the higher of percentage or cost depletion, never both [GPDm8NftR5U @ 00:03:25]. Tracy Lenz pushes owners off autopilot. After a recent inheritance or purchase, such as an asset with 18 newly drilled wells, cost depletion can win, and methods can be mixed property by property. Lenz's formula is basis divided by barrels remaining, times barrels sold, with the switch point at roughly $9 to $10 per barrel [NYvxAlVlAmQ @ 00:39:29]. Matt Sands relays a listener-CPA tip that an inherited step-up can accelerate cost depletion. Sands limits the play to substantial interests, because the appraisal and EUR work costs a couple thousand dollars [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:13:42]. The allowance itself has long been a political target. In a historical debate clip, Senator Kennedy was pressed on whether the 27.5% allowance was a conspicuous loophole. The senator answered that about 104 commodities carry depletion allowances and that smaller producers were having hard times, and noted a past vote to reduce the allowance only for the largest producers [NAcWqXJVAcs @ 00:01:18]. Lenz tracks two pending bills today, one raising the marginal-well limit from 1,000 to 2,000 barrels, but expects neither to move.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Non-op working interest bleeds cash in ways royalty owners never see. Tracy Lenz walks through the math: $800 of monthly revenue against $1,000 of operator charges, including JOA overhead with COPAS escalation, nets the owner negative $200 every month. The owner cannot force a shut-in and can only audit the operator. Declining to participate triggers roughly a 300% non-consent penalty, and plugging and abandonment at $30,000 to $40,000 per well can make the interest unsellable [mHolW0RfGQ0 @ 00:06:58]. Matt Sands sees that liability land on clients who inherited non-op working interest from an uncle or grandfather, bringing environmental, financial, and plugging exposure they never chose [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:18:02]. On the buy side, Troy Eckard warns that new promoters with no track record are flooding in and marking interests up four to five times, so $100,000 may buy only $20,000 of real interest [41VgsNOdrto @ 00:07:09]. Toby Mathis adds the drilling and liquidity risk. Exploration outfits can see two or three of ten wells come up dry, the money is illiquid, and payback can stretch five to seven years, or about eleven [TfG5auc0OXc @ 00:11:25].

Inheritance is where royalty checks die quietly. Royalty Clerk's Walt scenario starts with a Texas owner who died three years ago without a will. The checks stopped because Texas law lets the operator hold royalties without interest while ownership is in reasonable doubt, and the most common affidavit-of-heirship failure is a missing child [q5XqULtWaUQ @ 00:03:25]. Matt Sands and Justin Williams put a price on that freeze: operators hold royalties in suspense until heirship is decided, and clearing it usually costs several thousand dollars in each state where the minerals sit [cO3OBCezwjw @ 00:10:28]. Williams lived the worst version. Family lore contradicted the will and trust, a marital share split the interests, and title disputes locked up nearly all payments [cO3OBCezwjw @ 00:27:04]. The same hosts warn that recorded deeds trigger unsolicited offers, and the first offer can leave money on the table. Fractionalization from 100% to 50%, 25%, 12.5%, and 6.25% makes buyers discount, because one net mineral acre takes the same work as a hundred. Tim Pawul's list of owner mistakes includes not knowing what you own, decimal errors as small as 0.00000786% versus 0.00000797%, and money left in suspense, citing one recovery of $10 million [mcQ5KsrbKzc @ 00:44:56].

The tax traps hit cash flow before they hit the return. Matt Sands and Justin Williams report that without a W-9 and tax ID on file, operators withhold roughly 30% by law. A lease with no post-production deductions does not exempt you from severance, ad valorem, or production taxes. In their own acquisition, the prior owner kept receiving the county bill while penalties accrued, though penalties may be negotiable if you show you were never notified [_MHogbd2xzU @ 00:16:53]. The same hosts flag the opposite problem: once the tax ID is in, nothing is withheld, so owners must set aside cash and make estimated payments. A zero basis at sale means the entire proceeds are taxed [z9gHz7FYvRk @ 00:06:35]. Scott warns that IDC is recaptured as ordinary income on sale, and that K-1s arrive in June or July, so you should file an extension. Working and royalty interests should never share one entity, though the time value of money still favors taking the deduction [J21M9DVmwY8 @ 00:27:58]. Neil Jesani Tax Advisors adds that royalty income is ordinary income and is also exposed to the net investment income tax [FagQvbKX71g @ 00:04:01]. Each of these hits lands even when the wells perform exactly as planned.

chapters.question_prompt: Who regulates drilling and spacing, and how do commission hearings, permits and court disputes affect mineral owners?
chapters.title: Regulators, Hearings and Permits
chapters.subtitle: What the Texas Railroad Commission does, its open meetings, elections, RRC CASES and permit search, New Mexico OCC rulemaking and OCD docket hearings, well spacing, Marcellus permitting, Southfield drilling-permit protests, and the Oasis Pipeline v. Penn Virginia appeal
chapters.executive_summary: Operators, regulators, and opponents appearing before New Mexico's Oil Conservation Commission, the Texas Railroad Commission, New York's DEC, and Michigan's DEQ keep landing on the same point: the permit and the docket clock control the money. Operator witnesses McGowan and Sporich both reject 30-day windows and want roughly 90 days. Both attack bonding triggers that McGowan says can push a 100-well operator to $15 million overnight. The street mechanics run through W-1 permits, API numbers, the RRC GIS viewer, and the RRC CASES portal. They also cover tiered blanket bonds from $150,000 to $1 million and area-of-review fights ranging from a half mile to 10 miles. The disagreement is sharp. Public commenters put average plugging at $163,000 and want transfers frozen until cleanup. Small operators say cash bonds and transfer approvals will run independents out of the state.

sections.title: 1. The Practitioner Consensus: Regulatory Clocks, Bond Exposure, and the Permit as the Real Lever
paragraphs: Every operator-side witness in Santa Fe made the same complaint: regulatory clocks run shorter than real deals and real engineering. McGowan, an operator and reservoir engineer, told the Oil Conservation Commission that the proposed 30-day window is too short. He wants 90 days plus a grace period to cover complex projects, OCD data requests, and third-party consultants, and he summed it up as 'I like 90 days better than 30' [gfqoliQ78bk @ 00:04:45]. He went further on the 12-month marginal-well window. His own deal negotiation had already taken one year, with roughly 6 more months needed to raise capital. He said he would 'love' 5 years and cited transient flow, decline curves, and Fetkovich [gfqoliQ78bk @ 01:01:06]. NMOGA's Clayton Sporich, who co-founded Tap Rock and left as EVP Land and Legal, landed in the same place. He called 30 days inadequate and said the right number is 'closer to 90 days,' with a 5-year or 15-month presumption as fallbacks [gfqoliQ78bk @ 01:42:23]. In the Devon versus Perian special docket, Holiday flagged the 30-day proposal and 20-day notice periods before the deadlines were locked [Gyi9ijeMNgA @ 01:26:09]. In Texas, Commission Shift reported that producing regions sit 2 to 7 hours from Austin, which is why the group pushed the Railroad Commission to take remote public input over the conference phone [fqz-wQBuZ2A @ 00:01:29].

Both sides of the New Mexico bonding fight agree that the money question turns on marginal and inactive wells and on who ends up holding them. Sporich wants to keep the risk-based individual and tiered blanket bonds. He pointed out that the state reclamation fund held just over $66 million in April while federal grants were used instead, and argued that the fund should be the alternative to excessive bonding [gfqoliQ78bk @ 01:54:30]. McGowan put a number on the operator side. A 15% marginal trigger turns a 100-well operator carrying 15 marginal or inactive wells into '$15 million overnight,' and he warned that operators may simply 'hand you the keys and walk off' [gfqoliQ78bk @ 00:54:15]. During public comment, Krukauskas of a small family-owned Southeast New Mexico operator said cash bonds waste capital. He added that state approval of well transfers hurts small producers, and that the rule could 'run every small independent operator out of our state' [-7pNwWErBfk @ 00:04:29]. From the other side, Sheely of Gallup said about 95% of wells are plugged properly. Sheely estimated exposure at 5,000 at-risk wells times $163,000, or about $815 million, and said sellers dump marginal wells on 'poorly funded companies' [-7pNwWErBfk @ 00:13:27]. Operators and opponents disagree on the remedy. They agree that tired wells moving to thin balance sheets are where the plugging liability lands.

Regulators in three states treat the permit itself as the real enforcement weapon, and practitioners on every side organize around it. Greg Sovas spent 33 years at New York's DEC, the last 22 running the Division of Mineral Resources. He said his shop chose fixes over fines and withheld new permits from operators who did not clean up. He called that 'legal probably not' but 'effective very,' and summed it up as 'what do we care about a fine a penalty we got the environment cleaned up' [_C039ie8UHw @ 00:21:35]. In Texas, Commission Shift reported that the Railroad Commission revoked Blackbuck's 'True Blue' saltwater disposal permit in the North Culberson-Reeves seismic response area. The revocation followed quakes over magnitude 3, and a fault lay within a quarter mile; a lawsuit is likely [fqz-wQBuZ2A @ 00:03:32]. Alpha Seven Energy tells its roughly 200 investors to do their own due diligence by checking the permits and ownership on file at the Commission [gjm7ZmMazmc @ 00:00:28]. In Southfield, Michigan, the DEQ approved drilling at Word of Faith Church. The city still kept a temporary drilling moratorium running until late April and said it would request a temporary restraining order if necessary [Wvs9BxP1JfA @ 00:01:21]. Across all four venues, a state permit opens the fight rather than ending it.

sections.title: 2. Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Dockets, Permit Files, and Hard Permit Conditions
paragraphs: Hearings are won or lost in the filing layer before anyone testifies. The RRC CASES portal handles hearing requests, pre-hearing requests, appearance slips, and e-consent. Users can search by the last 4 digits of a docket number, the 8-digit case number, the operator, or the district. Dockets route to Legal Enforcement and Hearings, and the help line is 512-463-7158 [dgKvg8N8xd8 @ 00:00:41]. Missing a deadline is not always fatal. Fox moved to exclude Sporich's rebuttal because NMOGA filed it September 19 against a September 15 deadline and identified no direct testimony, yet the hearing officer declined to exclude it [gfqoliQ78bk @ 01:27:18]. Examiners do police scope hard. In the Devon versus Perian special docket, the examiner limited further Third Bone Spring testimony and denied a bid to recall Curry as 'not rebuttal.' The examiner then set a notice update for November 5, amended exhibits for the 12th to 14th, and closing arguments for the 25th [Gyi9ijeMNgA @ 01:29:20]. On appeal the clock tightens further. The Texas First Court of Appeals gave Oasis Pipeline and Penn Virginia 20 minutes each, with the appellant reserving 5 for rebuttal. The argument turned on whether 'seller's gas supply' covered frozen wellheads during Winter Storm Uri [oigm_h7P_sc @ 00:06:46].

Alpha Seven Energy's walk-through is the cleanest street-level permit audit taught. First, pull the W-1 drilling permit and its API number, then locate the well and its offsets on the RRC GIS viewer [gjm7ZmMazmc @ 00:04:22]. Their Roberts County design on the Mesa Vista Ranch kicks off around 2,800 feet, goes to about 8,500 feet, and runs a 5,000-foot lateral with a multi-stage frac. Alongside the permits, they pitch roughly 24,000 acres with room for up to 60 pads. Over 60 wells have been drilled and about 47 produce from the Granite Wash [gjm7ZmMazmc @ 00:08:39]. On the title side, Stump verified the Penrose-to-Perian chain of title during rebuttal. The landman witness warned that Lee County's online records run about 2 months behind, so recent conveyances may not show up in a remote search [Gyi9ijeMNgA @ 01:16:29]. For spacing exhibits, Enverus markets the spacing analytic inside Prism. It shows wells per section across the Lower Spraberry, Wolfcamp A, and Wolfcamp B, with a dynamic gun barrel viewer, and splits zone-specific spacing from multi-bench 'wine rack' spacing. It also bins type curves by boundedness and parent or child status, and its type curves show child wells are 'significantly impacted' [2rbY0Lt22CU @ 00:02:50].

The hard numbers sit in the permit conditions on injection and storage. After the Blackbuck revocation, Commission Shift reported that the Railroad Commission expanded the area of review from a quarter mile to a half mile plus a 2-mile review. It also cut maximum injection pressure where orphan or inactive wells sit nearby [fqz-wQBuZ2A @ 00:10:33]. In New Mexico's Class 6 primacy hearing, Dr. Helm Clark proposed a 10-mile radius and said the mean area of review in the permits reviewed was 8 miles. Clark also pushed for a 0.5-mile buffer around schools and hospitals, a cement temperature log run before the cement cures, through-casing resistivity logging, and at least one year of soil-gas baseline [_pyC_AisrQA @ 00:36:56]. Under questioning, Clark conceded that the director already has case-by-case authority to lower the pressure limit, as Ohio did on the Redbird #4 well. That undercuts a blanket cut from 90% to 80% [_pyC_AisrQA @ 00:31:02]. Sovas described New York's review as starting with casing and cementing, followed by an on-site visit. Aquifer wells need three strings, with DEC staff witnessing cement returns. The 2008 law set 330-foot setbacks and requires a 640-acre unit to be fully drilled within 3 years [_C039ie8UHw @ 00:19:40].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in the New Mexico rulemaking is over who carries plugging risk and how fast the bill arrives. Operator witness McGowan ran the 15% trigger on a 100-well company with 15 marginal or inactive wells and got a blanket bond of "$15 million overnight," dismissed the 30% alternative as "speculation… just a guess," and pushed incremental, risk-adjusted bonds or a higher threshold instead [gfqoliQ78bk @ 00:54:15]. NMOGA's Clayton Sporich ran a different playbook: keep the existing risk-based individual and tiered blanket bonds, reject the CPI escalator, and treat the reclamation fund as "an alternative to excessive bonding" [gfqoliQ78bk @ 02:34:33]. Public commenters attacked from the opposite flank. Rossi of Moms Clean Air Force cited an LFC average plugging cost of $163,000, some wells above $700,000, more than $100 million already spent by taxpayers, and up to $1.6 billion unfunded, adding that nearly nine in ten voters back full cleanup [-7pNwWErBfk @ 00:01:06]. Dueweke of the Sierra Club turned the capital-lockup complaint around: unspent bond money is refunded, so "only irresponsible polluters will be harmed," and every plug the taxpayer funds is an industry subsidy [-7pNwWErBfk @ 00:28:41]. Same wells, same plugging math, opposite conclusions about who should front the cash.

Whether a permit actually ends the fight depends on the state. In Michigan, the DEQ approved drilling by Word of Faith Church on its own property in a residential area and said the project met all of its requirements; days later an Oakland County judge issued a temporary restraining order that stayed in effect until the Wednesday hearing, while about two dozen protesters lined Evergreen and vowed to return to the church every Sunday [K4HrSTGgbFs @ 00:00:43]. Southfield stacked a temporary drilling moratorium running until late April on top of that and told reporters it would request its own TRO if necessary, since the operator only has to notify the state five days before drilling [Wvs9BxP1JfA @ 00:01:21]. Former New York DMR director Greg Sovas described the opposite architecture: the 1981 law Sovas helped author replaced a bare "notice of intention" with permits and fees and superseded local rules except for taxation and roads [_C039ie8UHw @ 00:16:02]. In Texas, the procedural lever cuts toward the operator: after the RRC revoked Blackbuck's True Blue disposal permit, Commission Shift reported that simply filing a hearing request may allow injection to resume [fqz-wQBuZ2A @ 00:13:33]. The playbook is jurisdictional: local injunctions bite in Michigan, state preemption shields wells in New York, and hearing requests buy time in Texas.

Practitioners also split on how much downhole proof a regulator should demand before trusting a wellbore. McGowan opposed blanket caliper and casing-integrity log runs on older inactive wells, arguing that a well cemented to surface, or one completed with a DV-tool two-stage cement job, is already "bulletproof" [gfqoliQ78bk @ 00:16:54]. On the Class VI side, Dr. Helm Clark argued for more logging, not less: set the cement and run a temperature log before it cures, "because when cement sets, it's an exothermic reaction" [_pyC_AisrQA @ 01:14:25]. Yet Helm Clark retreated on monitoring wells that penetrate the injection zone, pointing to ADM, where the gauges at the perforations "all failed" and the monitoring wells were eventually pulled out of the injection zone [_pyC_AisrQA @ 00:17:16]. The 10-mile review radius followed the same arc. Helm Clark picked 10 miles as half the farthest 20-mile incident distance because 20 miles "just seemed too extreme," while the commission countered that the mean area of review in the permits reviewed already ran 8 miles, and Helm Clark ultimately conceded the extra radius is "unnecessary" if the area of review is that large [_pyC_AisrQA @ 00:40:32]. McGowan wants fewer blanket log runs; Helm Clark wants more logs but fewer blanket radii. Neither defends a one-size mandate.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure McGowan described is not a blowout; it is a balance-sheet event. Under the 15% trigger, an operator with 100 wells and 15 marginal or inactive ones sees the blanket bond become "$15 million overnight," and McGowan warned operators may simply "hand you the keys and walk off" rather than post it [gfqoliQ78bk @ 00:55:11]. Concentration compounds the problem: McGowan could not borrow against a single well, described "a million and a half barrel well," and put the exposure at "$50 million for one operator" [gfqoliQ78bk @ 00:57:44]. Public commenters documented where those keys end up. Sheely of Gallup said about 95% of wells are plugged properly but estimated 5,000 at-risk wells at $163,000 each, roughly $815 million against the LFC range of $700 million to $1.6 billion, and said sellers dump marginal wells on "poorly funded companies" [-7pNwWErBfk @ 00:13:27]. Jones of Citizens Caring for the Future pointed to the Carlsbad brine-well sinkhole: 14 years to fix, with the company bankrupt two years in [-7pNwWErBfk @ 00:09:23]. The economics check is blunt: a buyer picking up a marginal-heavy package inherits the bond step-up and the plugging tail at once, and the weakest buyers are exactly where commenters say those packages land.

Several witnesses lost ground on cross-examination through their own paperwork. Under questioning by applicants' counsel Tisdale, NMOGA's Clayton Sporich conceded that the trade group's redline used a five-year no-production presumption while Sporich's own direct testimony defended the existing 15-month standard, answering simply "they do conflict" [gfqoliQ78bk @ 03:21:28]. Minutes later Sporich admitted misreading the $200,000 bond figure, an admission that undercut the bonding critique built on it [gfqoliQ78bk @ 03:36:18]. In the Devon–Perian pooling fight, the Devon reservoir engineer had to walk the examiner through a tangle of facility costs: $3.15 million per well if only two wells are drilled, $2.21 million in the updated AFE, a $1.27 million figure that was a "clerical error" for the $1.3 million full credit back, and a $2.56 million average, insisting these were three values, not six [Gyi9ijeMNgA @ 00:25:33]. Later in the same docket, a request to recall Curry was denied outright as "not rebuttal," closing off a chance to repair the record [Gyi9ijeMNgA @ 01:22:04]. Every one of these slips came from numbers or positions already on file, and every one handed opposing counsel a clean impeachment line in front of the examiner or the commission.

Winter Storm Uri produced the costliest contract trap on the record. Oasis Pipeline told the First Court of Appeals that Penn Virginia shut in all 500 wells, and quoted PVA's own summary-judgment brief conceding "frozen equipment and frozen wellheads certainly were the central cause" of the non-delivery [oigm_h7P_sc @ 00:09:36]. Because the parties struck the NAESB safe-harbor language and added "other failure of production," Oasis argued the contract never required PVA to deliver "a single molecule" of gas, and that "the consequence under this contract is financial, not operational" [oigm_h7P_sc @ 00:51:19]. A force majeure declaration riding on transporter declarations is only as strong as the clause it sits in. Saltwater disposal carries its own reversal risk. Blackbuck's True Blue well in the North Culberson-Reeves seismic response area sat amid quakes over magnitude 3 with injection deeper than 9,000 feet; Blackbuck had relinquished six permits, injected 30,000 barrels a day in 2022, was suspended in January 2024, and lost the permit with a fault inside a quarter mile [fqz-wQBuZ2A @ 00:03:32]. Helm Clark's Ohio case showed the CO2 version: four undocumented 1930s wells led to brine damage in 28 wells after Redbird #4 began operating around 2017 [_pyC_AisrQA @ 01:36:32].

callout.title: Four Gates Before You Buy, Testify or Inject
callout.body: Each gate comes straight from a loss, reversal or impeachment a practitioner lived through on the record. Clear all four before committing capital or walking into a hearing room.
items: Run the marginal-and-inactive share of any acquisition package against the 15% bonding trigger before signing; McGowan's 100-well example hit $15 million overnight and operators may hand over the keys and walk off [New Mexico Oil Conservation Commission — gfqoliQ78bk @ 00:54:15].

Reconcile your redline with your direct testimony before filing; Sporich conceded the five-year redline and the 15-month testimony "do conflict" on cross [New Mexico Oil Conservation Commission — gfqoliQ78bk @ 03:21:28].

Audit every exhibit cost line for clerical errors before the examiner sees it; Devon had to explain a $1.27 million figure that was really the $1.3 million full credit [OCD Pecos Hall — Gyi9ijeMNgA @ 00:25:33].

Check gas composition against the takeaway limit before drilling the first bench; Devon faced roughly 13,500 ppm sour gas against a 10,000 ppm takeaway allowance [OCD Pecos Hall — Gyi9ijeMNgA @ 00:34:55].

Track contested matters in RRC CASES by the last four digits of the docket number, the eight-digit case number, the operator or the district [Railroad Commission of Texas — dgKvg8N8xd8 @ 00:00:41].
If a disposal permit is suspended or revoked, file a hearing request, which may allow injection to resume [Commission Shift — fqz-wQBuZ2A @ 00:13:33].

Push for midstream-shutdown days to be excluded from marginal-well clocks as force majeure, citing Snowmageddon, line switching and compressor scrambles [New Mexico Oil Conservation Commission — gfqoliQ78bk @ 01:05:23].
